# MARIANO LENZI
# TO THE COURAGEOUS LADY AU-
# RELIA PETRUCCI.

It was a very ancient custom of the writers of Egypt to dedicate the most holy books they wrote to Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio." Here, the author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth and the Roman Mercury, credited with inventing writing and the arts.</note>: because they believed that all the arts, all the sciences, and all beautiful things had been discovered by Mercury, and that to him, as the inventor of all things, it was fitting to give thanks for what man learned or knew. And for this reason Pythagoras, and Plato, and many other great philosophers went to learn philosophy in Egypt, and for the most part they learned it from the columns of Mercury <note>The "Columns of Hermes/Mercury" were legendary pillars inscribed with ancient secret knowledge, said to have survived the Great Flood.</note>, which were entirely full of wisdom <term>sapientia: a term implying a divine or higher form of knowledge rather than just academic learning</term> and doctrine.

I likewise, Courageous Lady, judge that whatever can be produced by those who have known the height of your soul is fittingly dedicated to you; and that their beautiful thoughts, nourished by your divine spirit, ought to return to you and labor as much as they can in honor of your name. This is because they learn true virtues from the example of your life no less than those ancient philosophers did from the columns of Mercury. For if one takes note of the nobility, height, and gentleness of your soul; if one observes the honesty, courtesy, and grace; if one considers the prudence, discernment, and wisdom; and finally, if one gazes upon each of your virtues one by one, it is certainly seen by refined <term>purgati: literally "purified," referring to minds that have been cleared of common ignorance or base desires</term> minds that your life is nothing other than a mirror and an Idea <note>A reference to the Platonic "Theory of Forms," where an "Idea" is the perfect, divine archetype of a virtue.</note> of the way others ought to live; and

<summary>In this dedication, Mariano Lenzi compares the noblewoman Aurelia Petrucci to the legendary pillars of Hermes, suggesting that her life serves as a perfect monument of virtue and wisdom for others to study.</summary>

In Renaissance courtly language, it was common to describe noblewomen using divine attributes to emphasize their perfection.</note> Recognizing, therefore, this common debt and my own, I have done like those who, being unable to satisfy a debt with their own resources, pay with those of others; for, desiring to release a part of this great obligation that I have toward you, and because of the poverty of my own wit <term>ingegno: a person's natural talent, intellect, or creative capacity</term> being unable to send you fruit born of myself, I send it to you born in the gardens of others: namely, the books of love by Master Leone, under the titles of Philo and Sophia <note>The main characters of the work: Philo (the lover) and Sophia (wisdom).</note>: a chaste subject of love for a chaste lady who breathes love; celestial thoughts for a lady who is adorned with celestial virtue; the highest understandings for a lady filled with the highest concepts. Though I estimate (whenever I think of it) that I make two gains at once that are not small: releasing part of this obligation to you, and placing Master Leone under obligation to me (if shadows <note>original: "ombre." You then, having become, as it were, the guardian of this work, by directing your ray toward it—as if toward a body most fit to receive light—will make it appear more splendid and more miraculous to the world.

# FIRST DIALOGUE ON LOVE,
## BY LEONE EBREO.

### PHILO AND SOPHIA
### INTERLOCUTORS.

<margin>Ph.</margin>
Knowing you, O Sophia, causes in me both love and desire.

S O. These effects that the knowledge of me produces in you seem discordant to me, O Philo; but perhaps passion makes you speak thus. 

P H I. They discord from yours, which are devoid of any correspondence <note>original: "correspondenza." Philo is suggesting that his feelings of love and desire are not being reciprocated or matched by Sophia’s own feelings.</note>. 

S O. On the contrary, they are themselves contrary affections of the will: to love and to desire. 

P H I. And why contrary? 

S O. Because we love those things we judge to be good which we already have and possess; and those that we lack, we desire. Thus, that which is loved is first desired; and after the desired thing has been obtained, love comes, and desire fails. 

P H I. What moves you to hold this opinion? 

S O. The example of things that are loved and desired. Do you not see that when we do not have health, we desire it? But we would not say we truly "love" it then. And once we have it, we love it, and do not desire it. Riches, inheritances, jewels—before they are possessed, they are desired and not loved; after they have been obtained, they are no longer desired, but are loved. 

P H I. Although health and riches cannot be loved when they are lacking because we do not possess them, nevertheless they are loved "to be had" <note>original: "s'amano d'hauerle." Philo is arguing that we can love the idea or the potential possession of something even if we don't have it yet.</note>. 

S O. This is an improper way of speaking: to say "to love," meaning to want to have a thing. That should be called "desiring" it. For love is of the thing itself loved... 

<summary>This page marks the beginning of the first dialogue, where Philo (representing the Lover) and Sophia (representing Wisdom) debate the philosophical definitions of love and desire. Sophia argues that desire is for things we lack, while love is for things we already possess.</summary>

Our mind is a mirror and an exemplar, or to put it better, an image of real things; thus, there is nothing that can be loved unless it is first found to exist in reality. **PHI.** You speak the truth: but for this very same reason, desire can only apply to things that have being <note>original: "essere." and for this reason the Philosopher <note>A common honorific for Aristotle, whose definition of "the good" as "that which all things aim at" is referenced here.</note> has defined the good as that which everyone desires, since knowledge pertains to things that have being. **SO.** It cannot be denied that knowledge precedes desire: but I would say rather that not only is every cognition <term>cognition (cognitione): the process of knowing or perceiving an object through the intellect.</term> of things that are, but also of those that are not: because our intellect judges a thing that is, as it judges it; and likewise another that is not. ->reach actual being: thus, as for those things that exist but we do not possess, in their state of existence they can be desired so that they may be possessed by us. So, all desire is either that one should be what one is not, or to have what one lacks. Do you see then how every desire presupposes in part being, and in part privation <note>In philosophy, "privation" refers to the absence of a quality that should naturally be present.</note>, and desires the completion of being that it lacks? Thus, desire and love are founded on the being of the thing, and not on its non-being. And for a thing to be desirable, three titles must precede it in order. The first is being; the second is truth; the third is that it be good; and with these it comes to be loved and desired. This could not happen if it were not first esteemed as good, for otherwise it would not be loved or desired. And before it is judged good, it must be known as true; and as it really exists before the act of knowing, it must have real being. For first the thing exists in being, then it is imprinted upon the intellect, then it is judged to be good, and finally it is loved and desired. And for this reason, the Philosopher <note>Original: "il philosopho." This almost always refers to Aristotle, the primary authority in Renaissance education.</note> says that being, truth, and good are convertible into one; <note>This refers to the Scholastic doctrine that Being, Truth, and Goodness are "transcendentals"—different ways of describing the same ultimate reality.</note> except that being is in itself; and truth is when it is imprinted on the intellect; and good is when it moves from the intellect and will toward the acquisition of things through love and desire. So it is that desire no less than love presupposes being.

# ON LOVE.

...they are very far from the truth: although commonly all desired things are said to be loved, because they are esteemed as good; but correctly speaking, those things that have no **being of their own** <note>The author uses the term "essere proprio" to mean individual, actual existence as an independent entity.</note> cannot be said to be loved, such as health and children when they are lacking. From this imagined existence, a certain kind of love arises, but its subject is not the actual real thing desired—since that thing does not yet possess its own existence in reality—but rather only the concept of that thing taken from its general existence.

<margin>
Imagined love
</margin>

<margin>
Three sorts of things: loved and desired
</margin>

The subject of such love is improper, because it is not true love, as it lacks a real subject; instead, it is merely simulated and imagined, because the desire for such things is stripped of true love. Consequently, one finds three sorts of love and desire among things: 

1. Some things are **loved and desired together**, such as truth, wisdom, and a worthy person when we do not possess them.
2. Others are **loved and not desired**, such as all good things already held and possessed. 
3. Some others are **desired and not loved**, such as health and children when they are lacking, and other things that do not have **real being** <note>original: "essere reale"; this refers to tangible existence in the physical world.</note>. 

Therefore, the things loved and desired together are those which are esteemed as good, have their own existence, but are currently lacking. Those loved and not desired are these same things when we already have and possess them. And the things desired and not loved are those which are not only lacking, but also do not yet have within themselves their own being upon which love could fall.

<margin>
Things loved and desired together; things loved and not desired; things desired and not loved
</margin>

**SO.** I have understood your discourse, which pleases me greatly; but I see many things that have their own real being, and when we do not have them, we desire them, but we do not love them...

->### DIALOGUE I.<-

[...tru]th; which I would like to understand. I mean to say, why is it that with the <term>useful</term><note>original: "utile"; referring to things pursued for their practical benefit or advantage, like wealth or tools</note>, love is not found together with desire? Instead, while it is desired, it is not loved, and once desire ceases, love begins. Yet with the <term>delectable</term><note>original: "dilettabile"; referring to things pursued for the sake of sensory or aesthetic pleasure</note>, we find the opposite: for as much as it is desired, it is loved, and when the desire ceases, the love also ceases. The cause is the different way of enjoying these two types of things, both loved <margin>where the useful may be</margin> and desired. Because the useful consists in the continuous possession of the thing, the more it is possessed, the more its utility is enjoyed. If possession is lost—and truly it ceases after it has been held—even if there is desire, there will not be love. But with the delectable, its delight does not consist in possession, nor in habit, nor in total acquisition, but in a certain attention mixed with a sense of lack. When that lack is entirely gone, the delight fails, and consequently the appetite and love for that delectable thing also cease. SO. It seems reasonable to me that desire requires the lack of the delectable, but it would seem to me that love requires the present enjoyment of it. Since one does not have love for that which is entirely lacking, one cannot yet have love even if there is desire; thus, the love of the delectable must exist only while it delights—not before, when it is lacking, nor after, when it satisfies. However, the useful and the delectable can only possess an intellectual rationale through the moderation and the "mean" <note>original: "mediocrità," referring to the Aristotelian Golden Mean—the desirable middle between two extremes.</note> of love and desire for them. 

This moderation is the only virtue to be found in those things; and missing that middle ground, whether by more or less, is a vice where the useful and delectable are concerned. For such loves, when stripped of reason, are wicked and vicious, belonging more to brute animals than to humans. The "mean" that reason establishes in this regard is the only true love. From that middle point, it is proven that the more excessively one desires, loves, and pursues it, the more truly it is a virtue; this is because such desire is no longer mere pleasure or utility, but depends upon the moderation of those things, which is an intellectual virtue and truly an **honorable thing** <term>honestà: In this philosophical context, this refers to moral nobility or "the Good," which is pursued for its own sake rather than for profit or pleasure.</term>.

But because <margin>why man is not satiated by power</margin> its delight is not material in terms of physical sensation, but spiritual, residing in the human imagination and thought, and also because it is joined with the useful, men who possess power are not satiated by it. On the contrary, kingdoms, empires, and dominions, after they are acquired, are loved and preserved with cunning and solicitude. This is not because they possess the virtuous—for in truth, virtue is found in few such desires—but because the human imagination, in which this delight consists, is not satiated like the material senses. Nor does our will love Him according to how worthy He is of being loved, but only as far as it can reach toward Him in the act of loving.

**SO.** Can a thing still be known if it is not fully comprehended by the knower?

Fire is comprehended by the eye, not according to its burning nature—for if it were so, it would burn the eye—but only according to its color and its shape. And what greater example is there than the fact that the great hemisphere of the sky is comprehended by so small a part as the eye? You see that its smallness is so great that one might find a wise man who believes the eye to be indivisible <note>original: *indiuisibile*; a reference to the mathematical or physical "point" which has no parts and cannot be divided further</note>, without the power to receive any natural division. Therefore the eye comprehends things according to its own ocular strength, its size, and its nature, but not according to the condition of the things seen in themselves. ### DIALOGUE I ###

<meta>catchword: Diuer= (Diversely/Different)</meta>

[...our] small intellect perceives the infinite God according to human intelligible capacity and strength, but not according to the bottomless sea <note>original: *pelago*; literally a "pelagic" or deep sea, used here to suggest an unfathomable depth</note> of the divine essence and immense wisdom. This knowledge is followed and answered by the love of God, in accordance with the ability of the human **will**, but not in proportion to the infinite goodness of that same most excellent God.

**SO.** Tell me, is desire mixed into this love of God?

**PHI.** On the contrary, divine love is never stripped of ardent desire, which is the desire to acquire what is lacking in our divine knowledge. In this way, as knowledge grows, so grows the love for the known divinity. Because the divine essence exceeds human knowledge in infinite proportion—and His goodness is no less than the love that humans bear Him—there always remains for man a happy, most ardent, and most unbridled desire to continually increase his divine knowledge and love. Regarding this growth, man always has the possibility to grow on the part of the object known and loved; although on his own part, such effects might be determined at a level beyond which man cannot reach further. Or perhaps, even after reaching the final degree, an impression of desire remains in him to know what he lacks, without ever being able to attain it—even if he were **blessed** <note>original: *beato*; referring to the state of souls who have achieved salvation and the vision of God</note>—due to the excellence of the divine object over human power and habit. Yet, such remaining desire in the blessed should not cause **suffering** <note>original: *passione*; in Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a "passion" or a painful state of lack</note> because of the deficiency, since it is not a human impossibility to have more; rather, it gives him the highest delight to have reached the limit of his possibility in the knowledge and love of God.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Philo and Sophia. # ON LOVE. #

<meta>catchword: con (with)</meta>

[Diverse] have been the opinions of men on the subject of **happiness**. Many have placed it in utility and the possession of the **goods of fortune** <note>Material wealth, social status, or luck, which are outside of an individual's direct control</note>, and the abundance of these as long as life lasts. But the falsity of this opinion is manifest: because such exterior goods are caused by interior ones, in such a way that the former depend on the latter; and happiness must consist in the most excellent things. This happiness is the end <note>The final purpose or ultimate goal</note> of all others, and exists for no other end, but all things exist for it; especially since such external goods are in the power of fortune, while happiness must be in the power of man.

Some others have held a different opinion, saying that **blessedness** consists in the **pleasurable**: and these are the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus; in this period, they were often characterized (sometimes unfairly) as focusing solely on physical or sensory pleasure</note>, who hold the mortality of the soul, and believe nothing to be happy in man except pleasure in whatever way it may be found. But the falsity of this opinion of theirs is not yet hidden: because the pleasurable corrupts itself when it reaches satiety and boredom, whereas happiness gives entire contentment and perfect satisfaction. Furthermore, we have said above that the end of the pleasurable is the **honorable** <note>original: *l'honesto*; referring to moral virtue or that which is good for its own sake</note>, and happiness is not for any other end; rather, it is the final cause of every other thing.

So, without doubt, happiness consists in honorable things, and in the acts and **habits** <note>original: *habiti*; from the Latin *habitus*, meaning a settled disposition or acquired quality of the mind</note> of the **intellectual soul**, which are the most excellent and the end of all other human habits; they are those through which man is truly man, and possesses greater excellence than any other animal.

**SO.** How many, and of what kind, are these habits of intellectual acts?

**PHI.** I say that they are five: **Art, Prudence, Intellect, Science**, and **Wisdom**.

**SO.** In what way do you define them?

**PHI.** **Art** is the habit of things to be made according to reason, and these are those things that are made with the hands and with...

This doctrine alone deals with spiritual and eternal things, whose being in nature is much greater and more fully known than the being of bodily and corruptible things—though they are less known by us than bodily things, because they cannot be comprehended by our senses as the others are. 

Thus, our intellect in its process of knowing is like the eye of a nocturnal creature <note>original: *spiritello*; in this philosophical context, it refers to a bat or owl. This is a famous Aristotelian metaphor: just as the owl's eyes are blinded by the sun but see well in the dim light of dusk, the human intellect is dazzled by the "brightest" truths of the divine and finds it easier to focus on lesser, material things</note> toward light and visible things; for it cannot see the light of the sun, which in itself is the clearest of all, because its eye is not sufficient for such brightness, and instead it sees the glow of the night, which is proportionate to it. This **Wisdom** and **First Philosophy** is that which reaches the knowledge of divine things possible to the human intellect; and for this reason it is called **Theology**, which means "discourse of God" <note>original: *sermone di Dio*; a literal translation of the Greek roots *theos* (God) and *logos* (word/speech)</note>. 

So it is that the knowledge of the various sciences is necessary for happiness, but happiness itself does not consist in those, but rather in a most perfect knowledge of one thing alone.

**PHILO.** Some hold that it is the **active intellect** <term>Active Intellect: in Aristotelian philosophy, the aspect of the mind that actively transforms sensory information into abstract concepts</term> which, by uniting <note>original: *copulandosi*; refers to the intellectual union or "coupling" of the mind with its object of study</note> with our **possible intellect**, allows us to see all things in actuality together in a single, spiritual, and most clear vision, through which the soul becomes blessed. The most illustrious philosophers reason about happiness in these ways; it would be a long task, and not suited to our current conversation, to recount everything they argue for and against.

Thus, they hold for certain that beatitude consists in the knowledge of the Divine Intellect, in which all things exist primarily and more perfectly than in any created intellect. ### DIALOGUE I.

...the sole object of our happiness, we love Him with **knowledge** and **love**, and the wise have differed in these two acts—that is, whether the proper act of happiness is *knowing* God, or rather *loving* Him: and it should suffice for you to know that both acts are necessary for beatitude <term>Beatitude: A state of supreme blessedness or perfect spiritual happiness, often used to describe the soul's union with God</term>.

*S O.* I would like to know the reasoning that moved each of the originators <note>original: *inuentori*; here meaning the proponents or founders of these philosophical schools</note> of these two opinions. 

*P HI.* Those who hold that happiness consists in **loving God** make this argument: that beatitude consists in the final act that our soul performs toward God, as that is the ultimate human end. And since it is necessary first to know Him and then to love Him, it follows that happiness consists not in knowledge, but in the love of God, which is the final act. They also support their view through **delight** <note>original: *dilettatione*; the spiritual pleasure or joy found in the presence of the beloved</note>, which is central to happiness and belongs to the will. Therefore they say that the truly happy act is voluntary—that is, the love in which delight consists—and not the intellectual act, because the latter does not participate in delight in the same way. 

The others, on the contrary, make this argument: they say that happiness consists in the act of the primary and most spiritual power of our soul; and as the **intellectual power** is more primary than the **will** and more abstracted from matter, it follows that beatitude does not consist in the act of the will (which is to love Him). Instead, they say that love and delight follow knowledge as accessories, but they are not the primary end.

*S O.* One reason seems no less effective to me than the other; yet I would like to know your determination.

*P HI.* It is difficult to seek to determine a matter so disputed by the ancient philosophers and modern theologians: but to satisfy you, I wish to tell you only this—

This kind of desire is called love; it is for things not yet held that one desires to possess, or rather for those already held that one desires to enjoy through union. Both are properly called "desire," but the second is more properly called "love." Thus, we define love as the desire to enjoy through union, or rather, the desire to be transformed through union into the beloved thing.

And returning to our purpose, I will say that first, that knowledge must be of God, as far as it can be had of a thing so immense and so high. Because we recognize His perfection, and because we are not sufficient to know it entirely, we love Him—desiring to enjoy Him with the most perfect unitive knowledge possible. This great love and desire causes us to be drawn away <note>original: *astratti*; describing a state of 'abstraction' where the soul is so focused on the divine that it loses awareness of the physical body</note> into such contemplation that our intellect is lifted up. In this way, illuminated by a unique divine grace, it reaches a knowledge higher than human power and human speculation; and it enters into such a union—

## DIALOGUE I.

Thus, just as the first <note>referring to the "imperfect" love mentioned on the previous page</note> love is the child of desire, so this perfect love is its father and true generator. When this love obtains what it desires, the love does not cease, even if the appetite and desire may cease; for when the effect is removed, the cause is not thereby taken away. 

This is especially true because, as I have told you, perfect desire never ceases—which is to enjoy union with the beloved person—because this is always joined with love and is of its own **essence** <term>Essence (essentia): The intrinsic nature or indispensable quality of a thing</term>. However, a specific desire and appetite for the amorous acts of the body ceases immediately because of the fixed limit that nature has placed upon those acts. And even if these acts are not continuous, they are nevertheless bonds of such love rather than an occasion to dissolve it. 

Therefore, you should not excuse yourself from the perfect love I bear you because of the defect found in the imperfect; for the love I bear you is not the child of desire, but rather desire is the child of love, which is its father. My first words to you were that knowing you caused in me love and desire; I did not say "desire and love," because my love never proceeds from desire, but rather preceded it as its cause.

governed. Because love, after it is born, is deprived of all reason, it is depicted as **blind and without eyes**. And because its mother, **Venus**, has beautiful eyes, it therefore desires beauty; reason judges the person to be beautiful, good, and lovable, and from this judgment, love is born. **Cupid** is also depicted as **naked**, because great love cannot be disguised by reason nor covered by **prudence** <term>Prudence (prudenza): The ability to govern oneself by the use of reason; one of the four cardinal virtues.</term> because of the intolerable pains it inflicts. He is shown as a **small child** because he lacks prudence and cannot be governed by it. He has **wings** because love enters the soul with speed and, with equal speed, makes the lover go to find the beloved person, becoming **abstracted from himself** <note>This "abstraction" refers to the Neoplatonic state where the soul is so focused on the beloved that it "forgets" to care for its own body.</note>. He is depicted **shooting arrows** because he wounds from afar and targets the heart as his specific mark. Furthermore, the wound of love is like that of an arrow: sudden, with a narrow opening but deep penetration; it is not easy to see, difficult to treat, and very grievous to heal. Ordinary reason does not allow this; instead, reason directs everything toward being able to live honorably. I could even tell you that many have sought to die joyfully for the love of their virtuous friends. I could give you many examples of these, which I omit only so as not to—

# OF LOVE.

...a barren sea. And without doubt, for one who lacks excellent love, few virtues keep him company. **SO.** God save you, O Philo. *Do you pass by like this without speaking?*

**PHI.** Do not be surprised, O Sophia, that since you have usurped my memory, I cannot remember these things.

**PHI.** My soul remembers only those things of yours which fill it with love and with pain; these others, though they are yours, are alien to my suffering.

**SO.** Be that as it may, I forgive your forgetfulness, but not your promise. And since we have a convenient time, let us sit under this shade, and tell me of the birth of love, and what was its first origin.

**PHI.** If you wish us to speak of the birth of love, it will be necessary in this present conversation first to tell you of the commonality <note>original: "comunitá," referring here to the shared nature or presence of love across all things.</note> of its being, and of its wide universality, and another time we will speak of its birth.

**SO.** Is the origin of a thing not prior to its universality?

**PHI.** It is indeed prior in being, but it is not prior in our <term>cognition: In philosophy, this refers to the process of acquiring knowledge. Philo is making an Aristotelian distinction: what is "first" in nature is often "last" in how we learn it.</term>.

**SO.** How so?

**PHI.** Because the common nature of love is more manifest to us than its origin, and from known things one comes to the knowledge of unknown things.

**SO.** You truly speak the truth, for the universality of love is quite manifest; since almost no human is stripped of it, neither male nor female, nor old nor young, and even children in their first awareness love their mothers and their nurses.

**PHI.** You do not know, then, of love more common than that of the human generation <note>original: "humana generatione," meaning the human race or humankind.</note>.

**SO.** Also in all irrational animals that reproduce, love is found between females and males, and between children and parents.

**PHI.** Not only is reproduction the cause of the love found in humans and other animals, but there are many other causes; nevertheless, love is not only...

### DIALOGUE III.

...in these; rather, its commonality <note>original: "communità," here meaning the shared presence or universal nature of love.</note> extends to many more things in the world.

**PHI.** I will tell you the one, and then the other. Animals, besides naturally loving things that are suitable in order to follow them, just as they hate unsuitable things in order to flee them, also love one another reciprocally for five causes:

*first*, for the desire and for the **delight of generation**, such as males with females;

*second*, for **generative succession**, such as fathers and mothers with their children;

*third*, for **benefit** <term>beneficio: In this context, it refers to an act of kindness, favor, or nourishment provided by one to another.</term>, which not only generates love in the receiver toward the giver, but no less causes it in the giver toward the receiver, even if they were of different species; for it is seen that if a dog or a goat nourishes a child, they have a very great love for one another, and likewise if it nourishes some other animal of a foreign species;

*fourth*, for the **natural quality of the same species**, or of another very similar one; for you will see individuals of every species of non-predatory animals keep company because of the love they have for one another; even the predatory ones, although they do not keep company so as to enjoy the whole hunt alone, nonetheless toward those of their own species they have respect and love so as not to use their natural and cruel ferocity or venomousness against them; and even among different species of animals some friendly similarity is found, such as the **Dolphin** with man, just as others are found who hate each other naturally, like the **Basilisk** and man, who kill each other with sight alone <note>The basilisk was a mythical creature believed to kill with its gaze; this reflects the Renaissance understanding of natural history.</note>;

*fifth*, for **continuous company**, which not only...

->### ON LOVE.<-

**SO.** You even say that love is not only common to animals, but also to other inanimate bodies, which seems strange to me.

**PHI.** Why strange?

**SO.** Because nothing can be loved unless it is first known, and inanimate bodies <note>original: "corpi insensibili"—literally "insensible bodies," referring to objects that lack the five senses.</note> have no cognitive power within themselves. Furthermore, love arises from will or appetite, and is imprinted in the senses; inanimate bodies have neither will, nor appetite, nor sense: how then can they have love?

**PHI.** Knowledge, appetite, and consequently love exist in three modes: natural, sensitive, and rational-voluntary.

**SO.** Explain all three to me.

**PHI.** Natural knowledge, appetite, or love is that which is found in non-sentient bodies, such as the elements <note>The four Aristotelian elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> and the mixed bodies composed of the elements that lack sensation, such as metals and types of stones, and even plants, herbs, or trees. All of these have a natural knowledge of their goal and a natural inclination toward it. This inclination moves them toward that goal, just as heavy bodies descend downward and light ones ascend upward, as if to a place of their own <term>proprio loco: In Aristotelian physics, every element has a "natural place" it seeks to return to (e.g., earth seeks the center of the world).</term> that is known and desired. This inclination is called, and truly is, appetite and natural love.

Knowledge and appetite, or sensitive love, is that which is found in irrational animals <note>Animals guided by instinct rather than reason.</note> for pursuing what is suitable for them and fleeing what is unsuitable, such as seeking food, drink, the right temperature, sexual union, rest, and similar things. These must first be known, then desired <note>original: "appetirle"</note> or loved, and finally pursued. For if the animal did not know them, it would not desire or love them, and if it did not desire them, it would not pursue them to obtain them; and without having them, it could not live. But these—

# ON LOVE.

*nature*. **SO.** What reason do you have to call those natural and sensitive inclinations "love"? For love would seem properly to be an affection of the **will** <note>original: "uolontà"</note>, and among all lower beings, the will is found only in humans. You should call those other things inclinations, or **appetite** <note>original: "appetito"—a term used in Renaissance philosophy to describe the innate drive or desire in any being toward its own perfection or preservation.</note>, and not love.

**PHI.** Things are known by their opposites, for, as **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristotile"—the Greek philosopher whose views on physics and logic heavily influenced the author's arguments here.</note> says, the science of opposites is one and the same. If the opposite of this exists and is called hate, then this should reasonably be called love. Just as in humans voluntary hate is the opposite of love, so in animals the hate of things unsuitable for life is the opposite of the love for things suitable for it; the animal flees the one and follows the other, because hate causes it to flee, just as love causes it to follow. And in **irrational bodies** <note>inanimate objects like rocks or water.</note>, there is a natural love of the heavy for the low <note>According to the science of the time, "heavy" things like earth or lead had a "natural love" for the center of the world, which was why they fell downward.</note>, and they follow it; just as they flee the other for hating it. The light body, on the contrary, loves the high and hates the low. And since hate is found in all things, so love is found in all things.

**SO.** How can one love, who does not know?

**PHI.** Rather, it knows because it loves and hates.

**SO.** And how can one know who has neither reason, nor sense, nor imagination, as is the case with these lower, insensible bodies?

...directed toward knowing its end and its proper places, so they are directed by that knowledge to love and desire them, and to move themselves to find them when they are separated from them. This love is also of the same sort as that which terrestrial animals have for the earth, maritime animals for the water, birds for the air, and the **Salamander** <note>Following ancient and medieval folklore, the author treats the salamander as a creature literally born from and living within fire.</note> for the fire, which is said to be born there and to dwell within it. ## DIALOGO II.

...friendship? <note>original: *amicitia*; this concludes the sentence from the previous page discussing the perfect balance required for the human soul.</note> Some call this friendship *harmony, music, and concord*, and you know that friendship creates concord just as enmity causes discord. For this reason, the philosopher Empedocles <note>A Greek philosopher who famously taught that the universe is governed by the two opposing forces of Love (attraction) and Strife (repulsion).</note> says that the causes of generation and corruption <note>original: *generatione, & corruttione*; in natural philosophy, "generation" is the coming-into-being of a thing, while "corruption" is its decay or dissolution.</note> in all lower things are six: the four elements, friendship, and enmity. This is because the friendship of the four contrary elements causes all generation of the composite bodies made from them, and their enmity causes their corruption. 

According to these four degrees of the generation of love that I have described to you—occurring within the four elements, which are the cause of the generation of all composite bodies across four degrees of composition—you must also understand that there are just as many degrees of hatred, which are the cause of their dissolution and corruption. Thus, just as every evil and ruin derives from the enmity of these four elements, so every good and generation comes from their love and friendship.

**SOPHIA.** I am pleased with the discourse you have shared regarding the manners and reasons of love found in this lower world—that is, in all things subject to birth and decay. This applies to humans as well as brute animals, plants, and those mixed bodies <note>Inanimate substances, like stones or liquids, formed by the blending of the four elements.</note> that possess no soul, as well as the four elements themselves and the **prime matter** <term>prime matter: or *materia prima*, the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality before it is shaped into specific things like earth or water</term> common to them all. I see clearly that just as one species of animal loves another and seeks its company, while hating and fleeing from another, so too among plants some species are found to be friends of others. They grow together, and when they are in each other's company, they sprout more healthily; yet they are enemies to others, and are spoiled when near them. We even see metals: one will accompany another in its mineral vein, while another will not; and...

### ON LOVE.

...ancient <note>The Italian text begins with "co", completing "antico" (ancient) from the previous page.</note> writers included the secrets of **<term>intellectual knowledge</term>** <note>This refers to *cognitione intellettuale*, the high-level understanding of spiritual or universal truths that transcends simple sensory observation.</note> within **<term>fabulous shells</term>** <note>original: "scorze fabulose." A popular Renaissance metaphor where the "shell" or "husk" is the literal story, and the "marrow" or "kernel" is the hidden philosophical meaning.</note> with great artifice, so that no one could enter therein except for those with an intellect suited to divine and intellectual matters—minds capable of preserving true sciences rather than corrupting them.

SOPHIA. I like this reason: that high and excellent things should be entrusted to high and clear minds, and would be debased in those who are not so. But tell me the other reasons for these **<term>poetic fictions</term>**.

PHILO. They did this for four other reasons as well. The first of these (and second overall) is for the sake of brevity, so that they might fold many meanings into few words. Such brevity is very useful for preserving things in the memory, especially when done with such artifice that, by remembering a single **<term>narrative case</term>** <note>original: "caso historiographo." In this context, "history" refers to the literal plot or "historical" layer of a myth.</note>, one might also remember all the doctrinal senses included within it under those words. 

The third reason is to mix the delightful narrative and fable with the intellectual truth, and the easy with the difficult. In this way, human fragility is first enticed by the pleasure and ease of the fable, allowing the truth of **<term>science</term>** <note>original: "scientia." In the 16th century, this meant any structured body of certain knowledge, including philosophy and theology.</note> to enter the mind with sagacity. This is how children are usually taught disciplined and virtuous things, beginning with the easiest parts—especially since both can exist together, one in the "shell" and the other in the "marrow," as they are found in **<term>poetic fictions</term>**. 

The fourth reason is for the preservation of intellectual matters, so that they do not come to be changed over the passage of time in the various minds of men. By placing such meanings under the cover of these stories, they cannot deviate from the boundaries of those tales. Furthermore, for even greater preservation, they expressed the story in weighty and strictly measured verses, so that it would not easily...

...is that they might not be corrupted; for **<term>weighty measure</term>** <note>The author uses a metaphor of "measure" or "proportion" to suggest that truth has a specific weight or gravity that cannot be sustained by those with "vicious" or undisciplined minds.</note> cannot endure vice. Other, more elevated minds eat, beyond this, the **<term>moral sense</term>**; and others still higher can eat, beyond even that, the **<term>allegorical food</term>**, consisting not only of natural philosophy but also of astrology and theology. 

Joined with this is another goal: since these poems serve as common food for every kind of person, they are more likely to be preserved in the memory of the multitude. Truly difficult things are tasted by only a few, and among those few, the memory of them can easily be lost should an age occur that leads men away from learning. We have seen this happen in certain nations and religions, such as with the Greeks and the Arabs, who, having once been most learned, have now almost entirely lost their **<term>sciences</term>** <note>In the Renaissance, *scientia* (science) referred to any organized body of knowledge or branch of learning, including philosophy and the arts.</note>. The remedy for this danger is the artifice of placing knowledge beneath **<term>fabulous songs</term>** and narrative accounts. Because of the delight they bring and the sweetness of their verse, they remain and are forever preserved in the mouths of the **<term>common people</term>**—of men, women, and children alike.

Similarly, the **Cretan Jupiter**, son of **Saturn**, who through the governance he exercised over those people—forbidding them from eating human flesh and other beastly rites, and showing them human customs and divine knowledge—was called **Jupiter** and worshipped as a god. In their view, he was a messenger of God and formed by Him, whom they called **Jupiter**.

They give the name **Jupiter** <note>original: *Iuppiter*</note> to the element of fire, **Juno** to the air, **Neptune** to the water and the sea, **Ceres** to the earth, **Pluto** to the depths of the earth, and **Vulcan** to the burning fire found within the earth. **SOPHIA**: This is very strange—that they call bodies that are neither living nor sensitive, and which lack a soul, "gods." 

**PHILO**: They call them gods because of their greatness, their renown, their works, and the primary role they hold in this lower world. ...those [elements] close to the center are heavy: from which contrariety depends every other contrariety of the elements. It could also signify that ancient and Platonic opinion <note>Plato’s view in the *Timaeus* suggests the heavens are composed primarily of fire to be visible, and earth to be tangible, though later Neoplatonists emphasized fire and water/air for transparency.</note> that the stars and planets are made of fire because of their brilliance, and the rest of the celestial body is made of water because of its diaphaneity and transparency. From this comes the Hebrew name for the heavens, which is *Shamayim*, and it is interpreted as *Esh-mayim*, which means in Hebrew "fire" and "water" <note>original: *scamayn, et s’ interpetra exmaini*; the author is using a traditional Hebraic etymology where *Shamayim* (heavens) is a compound of *Esh* (fire) and *Mayim* (water).</note>. According to this, Strife <note>original: *Litigio*</note> and contrariety ascended to heaven during the first creation because the heavens are made of fire and water; however, they did not remain there successively, but were instead cast down from heaven to dwell continually on earth, where successive generation occurs through continuous contrariety.

**SO.** It seems strange to me that in heaven there are contrary elemental natures, such as fire and water.

**PHI.** If the primary matter <term>primary matter: the formless, fundamental "stuff" of the universe before it is given specific shape or qualities.</term> is common to both the lower bodies and the celestial ones—as those thinkers and Plato also believe—it is not strange that some elemental contrariety is found even in heaven.

**SO.** Why then does it not decay, as the lower bodies do?

**PHI.** Plato says that the heavens are corruptible by their own nature, but divine power makes them indissoluble. He means this by way of the active intellectual forms that inform them; furthermore, because these celestial elements are purer, acting almost as the "souls" of the lower elements, they are not mixed in heaven as they are in the lower world. In heaven, fire is found only in the brilliant stars, and water only in the transparent parts. Thus, even if Strife <note>original: *il Litigio*</note> wished to ascend to heaven at the beginning of the production from the womb of Chaos, it was nonetheless cast down into the lower world, where its habitation is today. By those labors during the birth of Strife <note>original: *Litigio*; here personified as the first-born of the primordial gods, representing the initial separation and conflict of the elements.</note>, he means the natures of the four contrary elements; by the "heaviness," he means the earth, which is the heaviest; by "sweat," water; and by "fiery sighs," air and fire. As the cause and remedy for the exhaustion of these contraries, divine power produced from Chaos a second son, Pan—which in Greek means "All" <note>original: *Pan, che in greco ſignifica tutto*</note>. By Pan, he means universal nature, the coordinator of all things produced from Chaos, and the force that pacifies contraries and brings them into harmony. Thus, Pan was born after Strife, because concord follows discord and comes after it. 

He also produced with Pan the three sisters, the Fates, called Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, whom Seneca calls the Destinies <note>original: *fate*</note>. By these, he means the three orders of temporal things: the present, the future, and the past, which he says God made followers of universal nature. Clotho <note>original: *Clotos*</note> is interpreted as the "turning" or "revolution" of present things; she is the Fate who twists the thread that is being spun at this very moment. Lachesis is interpreted as "extension" <note>original: *protrattione*</note>, which is the production of the future; she is the Fate who attends to the thread that remains to be spun upon the distaff. Atropos is interpreted as "without return," which is the past, which cannot be turned back; she is the Fate who has spun the thread already gathered on the spindle. They are called *Parche* <note>The English term is "the Fates."</note> by way of their opposite, because they spare no one <note>This refers to a classic etymological pun: *Parcae* (Fates) comes from *parcere* (to spare), used ironically because they are famously unsparing.</note>. 

He says of Pan that he was placed upon a throne by the command of Demogorgon because nature carries out the divine order and its administration in all things. ### DIALOGUE II. ###

The historical sense of a woodsman of Arcadia who, being in love, gave himself to music and was the inventor of the **pan flute** <note>original: *fistula*</note> with seven reeds joined together with wax, undoubtedly has another higher and allegorical meaning. This is that **Pan** (which in Greek means "all" <note>original: *uuol dire tutto*</note>) is the **Universal Nature** that orders all worldly things. 

The two horns on his forehead, which reach up to the sky, are the two **Poles** of the heavens: the Arctic and Antarctic. The spotted skin he wears is the **eighth sphere** <note>In the cosmology of the time, the eighth sphere was the firmament containing the fixed stars, located beyond the seven spheres of the planets</note>, filled with stars. The fiery face is the sun along with the other planets, which are seven in total, just as there are seven organs in the face: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and the mouth. These, as we have said above, signify the seven planets. 

The hair and the long beard hanging over his chest are the rays of the sun, the other planets, and the stars, which hang down into the lower world to bring about all **generation and mixture** <note>Generation and mixture refer to the biological creation and physical combination of the four elements on Earth</note>. The lower and rough members are the elements and the inferior bodies, full of coarseness and crudity compared to the celestial bodies. Among these members, the feet are like those of a goat, because goat feet never walk in a straight path but go jumping and crossing in an unordered way. Such are the "feet" of the lower world—its movements and transformations from one essence into another happen transversally, without a fixed order, and are free from the orderliness of the celestial bodies. This is the meaning of the figure of Pan.

**SOPHIA:** I like this. But tell me also the meaning of his love for **Syrinx** <note>original: *Siringa*</note>, which is more relevant to our purpose.

**PHILO:** They also say that this Universal Nature—so great, powerful, excellent, and marvelous—cannot be without love; and therefore he loved the pure virgin, and in...

And Aether is called the father because it is the principal part of the heavens, both due to its greatness which encompasses all the orbs, and also—according to **Plotinus** following the mind of **Plato**—because it penetrates the entire universe. He posits that the universe is full of ethereal spirit, but that the lucid bodies <note>the stars and planets</note> are particular members of the heaven in the manner of the female, who is a part of the man, who is the whole. It is also called father because the aether is a more subtle and more spiritual body than the lucid bodies of the stars and planets. 

Whence **Aristotle** says that because the stars are of a thicker and denser corporeality than the rest of the heaven, they are capable of receiving and retaining light within themselves; this is a thing the orb <note>the transparent celestial sphere</note> cannot do because of its transparent subtlety. ...the nature of the planet with which it mixes: when mixing with a masculine planet, it is male, and with a feminine one, female. Among men, many were called **Mercuries**, especially certain Egyptian sages and physicians who shared in these Mercurial virtues. Because Mercury is a bright planet, they make him the son of **Heaven** and **Day** <note>original: "cielo, e di die"</note>, because he shares celestial substance with the light of day—since the light of all planets comes from the sun, which creates the day. 

He is the brother of **Venus**, because their parents are shared, and these two planets are closely joined; each of them completes its orbit in nearly the same amount of time—that is, in one year—and they always travel near the sun without straying too far from it, which is why they are called siblings.

They call him the messenger of Jove because he announces and predicts the future things that the almighty God intends to do; for this reason, and for his eloquence, they call him the **interpreter of the gods**. 

His **rod** represents the rectitude of the intellect <note>meaning the "uprightness" or honesty of one's natural talent</note> applied to the sciences; and the **serpent** that encircles it represents the subtle discourse that surrounds that upright intellect. Alternatively, the rod is the **speculative intellect** of science, and the serpent is the **active intellect** of prudence regarding moral virtues—for the serpent, by its sagacity, is a sign of prudence, while the rod, by its straightness and firmness, is a sign of science <term>scientia: in the Renaissance, this referred to organized, certain knowledge, rather than modern laboratory science</term>.

This is the meaning of Mercury stealing Apollo's cows, for **Apollo** signifies and creates powerful lords, and the cows are their riches and abundance. Furthermore, their low status ensures they are not harmed by the fury of great masters, because they offer no resistance. For this reason, their friendship is halfway and imperfect.

Nevertheless, if the signs are opposite in the zodiac at the greatest possible distance—that is, one hundred and eighty degrees—they have among themselves entire friendship <note>original: "intera amicitia"; given that the text immediately identifies these signs as "capital enemies," this is likely a printer's error for "inimicitia" (enmity), though some philosophical traditions argued that perfect opposites possessed a form of "relational" unity.</note>: because the position of one is opposite and totally contrary to the other; and when one ascends, the other descends; when one is above the earth, the other is below. And even though they are always of the same active quality—that is, both are hot or both are cold—nonetheless, they are always contrary in the passive quality: for if one is moist, the other is dry. This, joined with the opposite distance and aspect, makes them capital enemies, such as **Aries** with **Libra**, **Taurus** with **Scorpio**, **Gemini** with **Sagittarius**, **Cancer** with **Capricorn**, **Leo** with **Aquarius**, and **Virgo** with **Pisces**.

SOPHIA: I grant you that spiritual beings may love each other because the inferior loves the superior. PHILO: I was already about to respond to this second argument of yours, if you had only been patient. In this manner, spiritual beings love corporeal and material things in order to supplement their deficiencies with their own perfection, and to unite with them to make them excellent.

By being a "mover," He does not become equal to the others; on the contrary, He remains much higher and more sublime, just as His sphere is more sublime than those of the other Intelligences. And just as His heaven includes and contains all the others, so His power contains the power of all the other movers. Furthermore, if He were equal to them simply because He is called a "mover" like the rest, then according to the first group <note>referring to the thinkers mentioned on the previous page who doubled the number of Intelligences</note>, He would also be equal to the other final Intelligences for being, like them, the goal of the first mover. In conclusion, Averroes says that to posit more Intelligences than what the force of philosophical reason demands is not the mark of a philosopher, since one should not see further than what reason demonstrates.

S O P H I A : This opinion seems more limited to me than that of the first group. But what will this man say regarding what Aristotle affirms—and reason along with him—that the end <note>the "final cause" or purpose</note> of the sphere's mover is more excellent than the mover itself?

P H I L O : Averroes says that Aristotle means that the same Intelligence that moves is also its own end in its continuous motion. For it moves the sphere to fulfill its own perfection; in this regard, it is more noble for being the end <note>the goal</note> of the motion than for being the <term>efficient</term> cause <note>the "efficient cause" is the agent that actually performs the action, whereas the "final cause" is the reason why the action is done.</note> of it. Thus, this saying of Aristotle is rather a comparison between the two types of causality found in the same Intelligence: namely, the effective and...

<summary>Philo explains Averroes' monotheistic perspective on celestial mechanics, arguing that God is the soul of the outermost sphere and that the dual roles of "mover" and "goal" exist within a single Intelligence rather than being two separate entities.</summary>

<meta>ink bleed-through from verso on left margin</meta>

...their ultimate end and intent is their perfection. But since this perfection consists in their union with the divinity, it follows that their ultimate end is in the divinity and not in themselves; hence Aristotle says that this divinity is an end higher than their own, and not merely the perfection belonging to them and remaining within them, as Averroës <note>Averroës, the 12th-century philosopher from Al-Andalus, was famous for his commentaries on Aristotle, which Philo is here contesting.</note> believes.

S O P H I A. P H I L O. Most certainly. For their ultimate perfection, end, and true bliss do not consist in these souls themselves, but in their elevation and union with the divinity. Because the supreme God is the end of all things and the bliss of all intellectual beings, it does not follow that their own perfection is not also their ultimate end; for in the act of achieving happiness, the intellectual soul is no longer centered in itself, but in God, who grants it bliss through His union. Herein consists its ultimate end and happiness, and not in itself, so long as it lacks this blessed union.

S O P H I A. This subtlety pleases me, and I am satisfied regarding my first question; let us come to the second.

P H I L O. P H I L O. The doubt becomes even greater: because for an Intelligence separated from matter, its proper and essential act is to understand itself, and in itself all things together. ->## OF LOVE.##<-

<meta>catchword: with</meta>

*...in which act its happiness and its ultimate end must consist, and not in moving a celestial body, which is a material thing and an act extrinsic to its true essence.*

S O P H I A. It pleases me to see you "blooden my wound" <note>A medical metaphor common to Philo’s persona as a physician: he is exposing the depth of her misunderstanding or intellectual "pain" to ensure a more thorough cure through logic.</note> in order to heal it better later; let us have the remedy, then.

P H I L O. You have heard from me before, O Sophia, that the whole universe is one **individual** <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "individual" refers to an indivisible, organic whole—the universe viewed as a single living creature.</note>—that is, like a single person—and every one of these beings, whether corporeal or spiritual, eternal or corruptible, is a member and part of this great individual. Both the whole and each of its parts were produced by God for a **common end** in the whole, together with a **specific end** in each of the parts. It follows that both the whole and its parts are perfect and happy only insofar as they rightly and entirely fulfill the duties to which they are directed by the <term>Supreme Artificer</term> <note>original: *sommo opifice*. A reference to God as the master craftsman or architect of the cosmos.</note>. The end of the whole is the unified perfection of the entire universe designed by the **Divine Architect**, and the end of each of the parts is not merely the perfection of that part in itself, but that through its own perfection it may rightly serve the perfection of the whole. This universal end is the primary intent of the Divinity; every part was made, ordered, and dedicated for this common end more than for its own. Thus, if a part were to fail in such service—in those acts pertaining to the perfection of the universe—it would be a greater defect, and the part would be more unhappy than if it failed in its own specific act. In this way, a part finds more happiness through the common good than through its own, just as in a human individual: for the perfection of one of its parts, such as the eye or the hand, consists neither solely nor principally in being a beautiful eye or a beautiful hand, nor in the eye seeing much, nor yet in the hand performing many crafts, but first and principally with...

<summary>Philo explains the "organic" nature of the universe, arguing that the happiness of any individual part—whether a human soul or a celestial body—depends on its contribution to the perfection of the whole universe as intended by God.</summary>

->### DIALOGUE II. ###<-

<meta>catchword: heart</meta>

...consists in the eye seeing and the hand doing what is fitting for the good of the whole person. Thus, many times, to save the whole person, the part naturally offers itself and exposes itself to its own danger, just as the arm is accustomed to put itself before the sword to save the head. 

Since this law is always observed in the universe, the <term>Intelligence</term> <note>In Renaissance cosmology, "Intelligences" were spiritual, angelic beings responsible for the movement of the planets and stars.</note> finds more happiness in moving the celestial orb—which is an act necessary for the existence of the whole, even if it is an external and bodily act—than in its own intrinsic, essential understanding, which is its own proper act. P H I L O. You have spoken well, and so it is the truth. Since our souls are spiritual and intellectual, no benefit could come to them from a fragile and corruptible bodily society that would not be far surpassed by remaining in their own intrinsic and pure intellectual act. ->### ON LOVE. ###<-

PHILO. You see it, or you know it.

...they are lovers, but I am only a lover, and not loved, and you are only loved, and not a lover; how do you want love to unite us?

And so you are always like the Laurel, green and fragrant, in whose fruit no other flavor but bitter and harsh is found, mixed with a stinging juiciness to those who taste it. Thus, to me, you have entirely become a Laurel; and if you wish to see the sign of your laurel conversion, look at my silent <note>original: "sorda," literally "deaf," but here meaning a mute or un-resonant instrument.</note> lyre, <term>cetara</term> <note>A stringed instrument similar to a cittern or lyre, often associated with poetic inspiration and Apollo.</note> which would not sound if it were not adorned with your most beautiful leaves.

SOPHIA. That I love you, oh Philo, it would not be modest <note>original: "honesto," referring to social propriety and feminine honor.</note> to confess it, nor yet pious to deny it; believe what reason makes most fitting, even if you fear the opposite. And since the time now invites us to rest, it will be well that each of us goes to take it; soon we shall see each other again. Attend meanwhile to your recreation, and remember your promise. FAREWELL.

The previous page ended with Philo describing how Sophia's image has "pierced" his senses and taken "eternal habitation" in his mind, causing him to lose awareness of his surroundings.</meta>

<header># ON LOVE.</header>

...if I were sleeping, would you accuse me? SOPHIA: No, because sleep would excuse you, as it is accustomed to take away the senses. PHILO: The cause that has taken them from me excuses me no less. SOPHIA: What thing could take them away as effectively as sleep, which is "half-death"? PHILO: The ecstasy or <term>alienation: a state where the soul is "alienated" or separated from the physical senses to focus on an internal thought</term> caused by amorous meditation, which is more than half-death. SOPHIA: How can thought abstract a man from his senses more than sleep, which casts him to the ground like a body without life? PHILO: Sleep causes life rather than taking it away, which amorous ecstasy does not do. SOPHIA: In what way? PHILO: Sleep restores us in two ways and is produced by nature for two purposes. One is to quiet the instrument of the senses and outward movements and to recreate the <term>spirits: subtle, vaporous substances believed to flow through the nerves and mediate between the soul and the body</term> that perform their operations; this is so they do not dissolve and consume themselves through the continuous labors of wakefulness. The other purpose is to allow the nature of those spirits and <term>natural heat: the internal warmth considered the primary tool of the soul for digestion and life</term> to be used in the digestion of food. To perform this perfectly, nature induces sleep through the cessation of the senses and outward movements, drawing the spirits to the interior of the body to occupy themselves all together in the nutrition and restoration of the <note>original: "animale," meaning a living being possessed of a soul</note> creature. And that this is so, see how the heavens—because they do not eat and do not grow weary from their continuous movements—are always vigilant and never sleep. Thus, sleep in animals is a cause of life rather than a likeness of death. But the alienation caused by amorous meditation brings a deprivation of sense and movement that is not natural, but violent; in this state, the senses do not rest, nor is the body restored. Instead, digestion is hindered and the person is consumed. So, if sleep would excuse me for not having spoken to you or seen you, much more should I be excused by this alienation and ecstasy of love...

->Leone Ebreo.<-

<summary>Philo argues that his deep "amorous meditation" on Sophia's beauty is a state of ecstasy more profound and physically taxing than sleep. He explains the Renaissance physiological view that while sleep restores the body's "spirits" and aids digestion, love-induced trance consumes the body and disrupts its natural functions.</summary>

[Sleep] draws them inside, in order to withdraw with them the <term>natural heat: the innate bodily warmth believed to fuel biological processes like digestion</term>; it requires an abundance of this for the digestion that takes place during sleep. [for the lover] has no care or memory of himself, nor does he perform any natural, sensory, locomotive, or rational work for his own benefit; instead, he is entirely alienated from himself and belongs to that which he loves and contemplates, into which he is totally transformed. Since the essence of the soul is its own act, if it joins itself to intimately contemplate an object, its essence is transported into that; it becomes its own substance, and it is no longer the soul and essence of the lover, but only the actual <term>species: in Renaissance philosophy, the mental image or "likeness" of an object that exists within the mind</term> of the person loved. ### DIALOGUE III.

-> O iij <-

[the] sun: which, being one, is divided and multiplied through the expansion and multiplication of its rays, according to the number and diversity of the places to which it is applied. When, therefore, the spiritual mind (which is the heart of our heart and the soul of our soul) withdraws into itself by the force of desire to contemplate an intimate and desired object, it gathers the entire soul to itself, contracting entirely into its indivisible unity. With it, the <term>spirits: the subtle vapors or "pneuma" that Renaissance thinkers believed acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term> also withdraw, even if the mind does not use them; they gather in the middle of the head, where thought resides, or at the center of the heart, where desire resides. This leaves the eyes without sight, the ears without hearing, and likewise the other instruments without sensation or movement. Even the internal organs of nutrition slacken their continuous and necessary work of digestion and distribution of food; only the <term>vital power: the biological force centered in the heart that sustains life and basic functions (like the heartbeat) regardless of conscious thought</term> of the heart commands the human body, which I have told you is the uniform guardian of life. This power is intermediate in location and dignity among the powers of the human body, acting as the binder of the higher part with the lower.

**SOPHIA**: In what way is the vital power a bond, and how does it hold the middle place in location and dignity between the higher and lower parts of man?

**PHILO**: The location of the vital power is in the heart, which sits in the chest—the middle ground between the lower part of man, which is the belly, and the higher, which is the head. Thus, it is the midpoint between the lower <term>nutritive part: the biological functions responsible for growth and digestion</term> in the belly and the higher <term>cognitive part: the intellectual functions of the mind</term> in the head. Therefore, by its means, these two parts and powers are linked within the human being. If the bond of this power did not exist, our mind and soul would be torn away from our body during these most passionate contemplations; the mind would fly away from us, so that the body, deprived of the soul, would remain [dead].

**PHILO**: In this, the soul is inferior to the <term>abstract intellect: the faculty of pure, unchanging reason that exists independently of the body</term>; because the intellect is entirely uniform, without movement from one thing to another, nor from itself to things outside it. However, the soul, which is inferior to it (because it depends upon it), is not uniform; rather, because it is the intermediary between the world...

### DIALOGUE III.

...between the intellectual and the corporeal (I mean the medium and the bond by which one is connected to the other), it must have a nature mixed of spiritual intelligence and corporeal change; otherwise, it would not be able to animate bodies. Therefore, it happens that many times it departs from its intelligence toward corporeal things, to occupy itself in the sustenance of the body through its nutritive powers; and also to recognize external things necessary for life and for thought, by means of the sensory powers and actions. Yet sometimes it withdraws into itself and returns to its intelligence; it connects and unites itself with the abstract intellect, its predecessor, and from there it departs again toward the corporeal, and then returns to the intellectual, according to its current inclinations. 

And for this reason, Plato said that the soul is composed of itself and of another: of the invisible and the divisible. And he says that it is a **self-moving number** <note>original: "numero se medesimo mouente" — A classical definition often attributed to Xenocrates, a student of Plato, suggesting the soul is both a principle of order (number) and the source of its own activity (motion).</note>. This means that it is not of a uniform nature, as is the pure intellect; rather, it is a "number" of natures. It is neither purely corporeal nor purely spiritual, and it moves from one to the other continually. He says that its motion is circular and continuous: not because it moves from place to place physically, but rather spiritually; and through its actions, it moves from itself into itself: that is, from its intellectual nature into its corporeal nature, returning then to the former, always in this circular manner.

**SOPHIA**: I seem to almost understand this distinction you make in the nature of the soul, but if you could find some good example to better settle my mind, I would be grateful.

**PHILO**: What better example is there than that of the two heavenly Princes, whom the immense Creator made as <term>simulacra: images or representations that mirror a higher reality</term> of the intellect and the soul?

**SOPHIA**: Which ones are they?

**PHILO**: The two luminaries: the great one that makes the day, and the small one that serves the night.

**SOPHIA**: ...

### DIALOGUE III. ###

<meta>ink bleed-through from verso on left margin; catchword at bottom right is cut off or missing</meta>

...as a separable spiritual act, and not a corporeal one in the manner of a quality or a passion <note>passione: in classical philosophy, a "passion" refers to an accidental property or state that a subject "undergoes" or receives from an external source</note>. Furthermore, the diaphanous <term>diaphanous: a transparent medium, such as air or water, through which light can pass</term> is only a vehicle for the light, but not the subject <note>suggetto: the underlying substance in which a quality (like color or heat) is rooted</note> of it.

SO. Why not?

PHI. Because if light were a quality within the diaphanous medium as its subject, it would have the six conditions of a quality. First, a quality would spread through the whole subject one part after another; but light penetrates through the entire diaphanous medium instantly. Second, an incoming quality changes the natural disposition of its subject; but light causes no change in the diaphanous medium. Third, a quality extends only to a limited space; but light extends through the diaphanous medium without limit or measure. Fourth, once the source that forms the quality is removed, some impression of it always remains in the subject for some time—just as the heat remains in water after it is separated from the fire—but once the illuminating source is removed, nothing of the light remains in the diaphanous medium. Fifth, a quality moves along with its subject, but light, as an illuminating force, does not move along with the movement of the air or water in which it exists. Sixth, many qualities of the same kind in one object become confused and mixed, or are combined into one; but many lights do not combine into one. You will see that if you walk before two lamps, they produce two shadows; and if before more, they produce more shadows. Furthermore, if three or more lamps are placed at a small opening from different sides, you will see that they project three distinct lights through the opening in opposite directions.

All these things show us that light in the diaphanous medium, or in the illuminating body, is not a quality or a corporeal passion, but rather a spiritual act <note>atto spirituale: an active, non-material force or presence</note> actuating the diaphanous medium through the representation of the illuminator; and it is separable by the removal of that source. And not otherwise the—

<summary>Philo provides six philosophical arguments to prove that light is a spiritual act rather than a physical quality, noting its instant speed, lack of physical residue, and distinctness when multiple sources are present.</summary>

->[...in] beauty they exceed all other parts of the body. You will recognize their craftsmanship<-

The object of sight is the entire corporeal world, both celestial and inferior; whereas the other senses can only imperfectly comprehend a small part of the inferior world. The medium of the other senses is either flesh (as in touch), vapor (as in smell), moisture (as in taste), or moving air (as in hearing). But the medium of sight is the luminous, spiritual, **Diaphanous** <term>diaphanous: a transparent medium, such as air or water, that allows light to pass through</term>—that is, air illuminated by celestial light. This light exceeds in beauty all other parts of the world, just as the eye exceeds all other parts of the animal body.

The act of the other senses extends to very few aspects of the bodies they grasp. Smell only perceives the "stings" <note>original: "pongimenti"—referring to the physical stimulation or "pricking" of the sense organs by particles</note> of vapors; taste perceives the stings of the moisture in food and drink. Touch perceives the stings of passive qualities <note>passive qualities: the basic tactile properties like hot, cold, wet, or dry</note> with some small degree of common feeling, but it does so materially and imperfectly. In this way, the "species" <term>species: the sensory images or "forms" of things that enter our minds</term> of these three senses are merely nearby passions and stings.

Hearing, although it is more spiritual and operates at a distance, still only perceives the heavy and sharp blows of air moved by the percussion of one body against another; and it does so only at a short distance. Its species are greatly mixed with the "passion" of the strike and with physical motion. But the eye sees things that are at the furthest circumference of the world and in the first heavens. It comprehends all bodies, both distant and near, through the medium of light. It receives all their species without any physical "passion" <note>passione: here meaning physical suffering or being acted upon/disturbed by a material force</note>. It recognizes their distances, their colors, their brilliance, their sizes, their shapes, their number, their positions, their movements, and...

...thing of this world with many and particular distinctions: as if the eye were a spy <note>original: "spione"—meaning a scout or observer that gathers information for a superior</note> of the intellect, and of all intelligible things.
