->DIALOGUE III.<-

...divine ideas, or **forms** <term>forms: originally "specie," referring to the intellectual patterns or essences of things that allow us to categorize what we see</term>; likewise our intellect not only understands the forms of all things, but also illuminates all the other cognitive faculties of man; so that, although their knowledge is particular and material, it may be directed by an intellect that is not beast-like, as it is in other animals. And yet, the eye and the sun are not entirely similar, for the eye sees and does not illuminate, while the sun illuminates and does not see.

**PHILO.** Perhaps in this they are not so different; for our eye not only sees by the universal illumination of the **Diaphanous** <term>Diaphanous: the transparent medium, such as air or water, which allows light to pass through and connects the eye to the object</term>, but also by the particular illumination of the shining rays that rise from the eye itself toward the object. These rays alone are not enough to illuminate the medium and the object; nevertheless, without them, the universal light would not be sufficient to bring about actual vision.

**SOPHIA.** Do you believe, then, that the eye sees by sending its own rays out into the object?

**PHILO.** Yes, I believe so.

**SOPHIA.** In this you are no longer a **Peripatetic** <term>Peripatetic: a follower of Aristotle’s philosophy, named after the covered walkways (peripatoi) where he taught</term>, for **Aristotle** rejects this view; he maintains that vision occurs through the representation of the object’s form within the pupil of the eye, rather than by sending out rays, as **Plato** says. <note>This identifies a classic scientific debate of the Renaissance: "extramission" (light travels out from the eye) versus "intromission" (light enters the eye from the outside).</note>

**PHILO.** Aristotle did not prove his case against Plato, for I hold that in the act of seeing both things are necessary: both the emission of rays from the eye to grasp and illuminate the object, and the representation of the object’s form in the pupil. Furthermore, even these two contrary movements are not enough for vision without a third and final act: which is the eye, by means of the rays upon the object, conforming the received form of the object to the external object itself; and in this third act consists the perfect logic of vision.

**SOPHIA.** This opinion seems new to me.

**PHILO.** Rather, it is ancient...

**PHILO.** Not by a specific organ, for they possess only that of sight; but by seeing the movements of bodies, and of lips, tongues, and other instruments of the voice, they comprehend their meanings—just as you see many men do...

### DIALOGUE III.

<meta>catchword: part</meta>

...but in effect, it always has one entire half of its sphere illuminated by the sun.

**SOPHIA.** How is it, then, that it does not appear so?

**PHILO.** Because, as the Moon is constantly moving—either distancing itself from or approaching the sun—the light that always illuminates its half in a circular fashion shifts from one part to another. That is, it moves from its upper part to its lower, or from the lower to the upper.

**SOPHIA.** Which is called the lower part, and which the upper?

**PHILO.** The lower part of the Moon is the one facing the earth that looks toward us; we see it when it is entirely bright, or when a portion of it is. The upper part is that which faces the heaven of the sun <note>In the geocentric model used here, the "heaven" or sphere of the sun was located beyond the sphere of the Moon</note> which is above it; we do not see this part, even though it is illuminated. Thus, once a month the entire lower half is illuminated by the sun, and we see it full of light; this occurs on the **fifteenth day** <term>quintadecima: the midpoint of the lunar month, corresponding to the full moon</term>, because the Moon is then directly opposite the sun. At another time, the other half—the upper one—is illuminated; this happens when it enters into **conjunction** <term>congiontione: the moment when the moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun, known as a New Moon</term> with the sun that is above it, which then illuminates the entire upper part. The lower part facing us remains completely dark, and thus for two days the Moon is not visible to us. 

On the other days of the month, the illumination of the half of the lunar sphere appears differently. This is because, from the moment of conjunction, the light begins to leave the upper part and gradually moves to the lower part facing us as the Moon moves away from the sun. However, an entire half is always bright; whatever light is missing from the lower part is found on the upper part. We simply do not always see that illuminated half in its entirety. This continues until the fifteenth day, at which point the entire lower part facing us is bright and the upper part is dark. After that, the light begins to transport itself back to the part...

This is because the soul is composed of intellectual light and corporeal darkness, just as the Moon is composed of solar light and dark corporeality. The changing of the soul’s light is like that of the Moon shifting from the upper side to the lower side facing us, and vice versa. This is because the soul sometimes uses all the cognitive light it has from the Intellect for the administration of corporeal things. And just as when the Moon is full it stands in opposition to the sun, and astrologers say that it is then in a highly inimical <note>original: *inimicabile*; in Renaissance astrology, "opposition" (the 180° angle) was considered a "hostile" or difficult aspect</note> aspect with the sun; so too, when the soul takes all the light it receives from the Intellect and directs it toward the lower part of corporeality, it is in inimical opposition to the Intellect and distances itself totally from it.

The contrary occurs when the soul receives the light of the Intellect from the upper, incorporeal side toward the Intellect itself, and unites with it just as the Moon does with the sun during a **conjunction** <term>congiontione: the alignment of the sun and moon (New Moon), here used as a metaphor for the mystical union of the soul and the divine</term>. It is certainly true that this divine union <note>original: *copulatione*</note> causes the soul to abandon corporeal things and the cares associated with them; it then remains dark, like the Moon, on the in[ferior side]...

The other quarter follows the opposition: and from that point the upper part (which we do not see) begins to overcome the lower part (which we do see) in light. And this is the state of the soul when it moves from opposition toward <term>intellectual union</term><note>original: *coppulatione intellettuale*; the mystical re-joining of the human soul with the Divine Mind</note>: for once both parts are in the light...

Thus, the soul—so wretchedly eclipsed of intellectual light—is compared to the souls of brute animals and is made of their nature. But be that as it may, bestiality—whether in whole or in part—is the ultimate destruction and the greatest defect of the soul. It is for this reason that <term>David</term><note>Referring to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> says to God in prayer: *Deliver my soul from destruction, and my only one from the power of the dogs.* <note>original: *libera da destruttione l'anima mia, e dal potere esser de cani unica*; a paraphrase of Psalm 22:20. That is, by coupling and uniting itself with the intellect, the soul receives all the intellectual light into its superior part, while its lower, corporeal part remains dark; and the body, no longer illuminated by the soul, loses its being, and the soul dissolves...

# DIALOGUE III.

...tell me, Sophia, which is the lesser evil?

**SO.** The lesser evil is always the truth, rather than the false.

**PHI.** The lesser evil is always the secure, rather than the dangerous.

**SO.** Are you a philosopher, and yet you are afraid to speak the truth?

**PHI.** While it is not the mark of a virtuous man to tell a lie (even if it were useful), it is nevertheless not the mark of a prudent man to tell a truth that brings him harm and danger. Because when telling the truth is harmful, it is prudence <note>original: *prudentia*; here referring to practical wisdom or the ability to govern oneself by use of reason.</note> to be silent and rashness to speak of it.

**SO.** To me, that fear of speaking the truth does not seem at all honorable.

**PHI.** I am not afraid of telling the truth, but of the harm that might happen to me for telling it.

**SO.** Since you are so struck by the arrows of love <note>A reference to the classical image of Cupid’s arrows, which were said to strike the heart and cause the "wound" of desire.</note> (as you say), what more fear do you have of him? **PHI.** I fear a new punishment.

**SO.** What do you fear that could be new to you?

**PHI.** I fear that what once happened to Homer might happen to me, who lost his sight for singing in disfavor of Love. <note>original: *Homero*; Philo refers to a tradition that the poet Homer was blinded as punishment. Fourth, you ask who were its parents: that is, if it had only a father, or only a mother, or truly if it was born of both, and who they were—whether divine or human, or of some other nature—and of them also, what was its genealogy. 

And ultimately, for the fifth, you wish to know the end <term>end: the *causa finale* or "final cause"; the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists</term> for which it was born into the world, and what need made it be born; for the final cause is that for which every thing produced was produced, and the end of the product is the first in the intention of the producer, even if it is last in its execution <note>This is a fundamental principle of Aristotelian philosophy: a builder thinks of the house (the end) first, even though the house is the last thing finished.</note>. For that which has no being in any way cannot be known, and that which cannot be known can even less be desired. Therefore, whatever is desired must have "being" in the mind; and if it exists in the mind, it must also exist externally in reality—if not in actuality, then at least in potentiality within its causes. Otherwise, <term>cognition<note>The mental action or process of acquiring knowledge and understanding.</note></term> would be false. Thus, in every respect, love is nothing other than desire.

Hence, he held that Love is a great **demon** <term>daimon: in Greek philosophy, a mediating spirit between gods and mortals, not an evil entity</term>, a middle being between gods and men, which carries the good works and chosen spirits <note>The original OCR reads "inetti," but in the context of Plato's *Symposium*, this refers to the prayers and "elect" or "chosen" spirits of men.</note> of men to the gods, and brings the gifts and graces of the gods to men, for everything is achieved through the medium of love. Something is "in act" when it is fully realized, and "in potential" when it has the capacity to become that thing.</note> desiring beauty in its realized form. Thus, love is either a middle point between the beautiful and the ugly, or a composition of both, just as **potentiality** is a middle state between being and **privation** <term>privation: the absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present</term>.

...of Plato, who, being the great philosopher that he is, would deny that there is love in God? **PHI[LO].** Regarding that species of love which Plato discusses in his *Symposium* <note>original: "convivio," meaning a banquet or feast; here referring to Plato’s famous dialogue on the nature of love</note>—which is only the love shared among human beings—he speaks the truth when he says it cannot exist in God. This is what is primarily called "love," because that which is centered in the beloved is instead called friendship and benevolence. This love he correctly defines as the "desire for beauty." And such love, he says, is not found in God; for he who desires beauty does not possess it, nor is he himself beautiful; and to God, who is the Supreme Beauty, beauty is never lacking, nor could He desire it. Hence, He cannot have love—that is, love of that specific sort. But for us, who speak of love in general, it is necessary to include equally that which is centered in the lover—which presupposes a lack in the lover—and that which is centered in the beloved—which presupposes a lack in the beloved, and not in the lover. And for this reason, we have not defined love as a "desire for a beautiful thing" (as Plato did), but simply as the desire for something, or a desire for a good thing. This good may be something lacking to the lover, or it may be something lacking only to the beloved—such as the love a father has for his son, a teacher for his student, or a friend for a friend. And such is the love of God for His creatures: a desire for *their* good, and not His own. And regarding this second kind of love, both Plato and Aristotle <note>The text continues on the following page.</note> concede and say...

P H I. Each of them being transformed into the other, each becomes two—that is, both beloved and lover together—and twice two makes four. So each of them is two, and both of them together are one and four.

-># OF LOVE.<-

...nor regarding this will there be a need to tell you, although we will stray somewhat from our purpose. Aristotle says that first matter <term>First matter: *materia prima*, the most basic, formless substance that underlies all physical reality and has the potential to become anything.</term> could not be newly made, because everything that is made must be made from something; for all concede that from nothing, not a single thing can be made <note>original: *di niente nessuna cosa far si possa* (a reference to the Latin principle *ex nihilo nihil fit*).</note>. And if first matter had been made, it would have been made from some other thing, and that other thing would then be the "first" matter, and not this one; and since this process cannot go on to infinity <note>A classic philosophical argument against "infinite regress": there must be a starting point that wasn't caused by something else.</note>, one must grant a matter that is truly first and never made. Therefore, first matter is eternal, and so too are the generation and corruption <term>Generation and corruption: The natural processes of coming into being and passing away.</term> that occur within it. Because first matter is of an imperfect being, it must always exist under some substantial form; and the generation of the new is the corruption of the pre-existing. Hence, every generation must be preceded by corruption, and every corruption by generation—just as the generation of the chicken comes from the corruption of the egg. The generation and corruption of things is therefore eternal and without beginning; such that every egg was born of a hen, and every hen of an egg, and neither of them was absolutely first.

The heavens <note>Referring to the celestial spheres or the cosmos beyond the Earth.</note> seem eternal in themselves, because if they were generated, they would also be corruptible; and they cannot be corruptible because they have no contrary <note>In Aristotelian physics, change occurs between opposites (like hot and cold). Because the heavens were thought to be made of a "fifth element" or ether, they had no opposite to struggle against.</note>, as do the elements and the things composed of them. Corruption comes from the triumph of one contrary over another, and generation likewise is a movement from one contrary to another. It is shown that the heaven has no contrary because it is impassible <note>Incapable of being affected or changed by outside forces.</note> and immutable in its substance and quality; and its round shape, among all other shapes, is alone devoid of contrariety. Consequently, it is incompatible for circular motion to have a beginning;

This is true even in the first motion <note>The "first motion" refers to the movement of the *Primum Mobile*, the outermost sphere of the heavens in the Aristotelian model.</note>: for if it were generated, its generation—which is itself a motion—would be prior to the "first" motion, which is impossible. And since an infinite process cannot be granted in generated motions, one must arrive at a first eternal motion. Furthermore, time, which follows the first motion—because it is the numbering of the "before" and "after" of motion <note>Aristotle’s classic definition of time as the measurement of change.</note>—must be eternal like motion itself. This is because every instant is effectively the end of past time and the beginning of the future; hence, no instant can be assigned that acts as an absolute first beginning. Therefore, time is eternal, without ever having had a beginning.

Furthermore, since the end <term>End: Here meaning the goal, purpose, or *telos*.</term> of the Creator in the creation of the world was nothing other than the desire to do good, why then should this good not have been performed always? For surely no impediment could ever intervene to stop the Almighty.

...God who is supremely perfect.

**SOPHIA.** These reasons of the Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: A follower of the philosophy of Aristotle, who famously taught while walking about.</term> seem to possess great force, especially the theological arguments regarding the eternal nature of the divine Maker and the purpose of his voluntary production. But what will the Platonists say—and all of us who believe in the sacred Mosaic Law <note>The "Mosaic Law" here refers to the Torah or the Pentateuch, specifically the account of creation in Genesis.</note>, which posits the creation of all things from nothing at the beginning of time?

**PHILO.** We others say many things in our defense. We agree that, according to the laws of nature, nothing can be made from nothing. However, we hold that miraculously, through divine omnipotence, things can indeed be made from nothing. This does not mean that "nothing" is the literal material of things, in the way that wood is the material from which statues are made; rather, it means that God can make things anew without any preceding matter at all. 

And we say that even if the heavens and first matter <term>materia prima: In ancient philosophy, the fundamental, formless "stuff" that underlies all physical reality before it takes a specific shape.</term> are naturally incapable of being generated or destroyed, they were nonetheless created from nothing in the beginning through the absolute creation of divine omnipotence. Furthermore, even if the reciprocal generation of things, circular motion, and time naturally seem to reject having a beginning, they did indeed have one in that miraculous creation. This is because they are consequences of first matter and the heavens, which were themselves newly created. 

As for the nature of the Maker, we say that the eternal God acts not out of necessity, but through free will and omnipotence. And as for the purpose of His work, we say that although His purpose in creation was to do good, and besides...

### DIALOGO III.

...not only as an answer to the second part of your question, but to the first part together with the second. **SOPHIA.** Explain it to me, for I desire to understand.

**PHILO.** Plato, seeing that the world is a common formed substance <term>substance: In this philosophical context, substance (sustantia) refers to the underlying reality or "stuff" that makes up a thing.</term>, and that each of its parts is likewise a part of that common substance shaped by its own specific form, rightly recognized that the whole, as well as each of its parts, was composed of a thing—or formless substance—common to all, and of a specific form that gives it shape.

**SOPHIA.** You are right; pray, go on.

**PHILO.** He judged that this formation of things, both of the whole and of every one of the parts, was of necessity new and not from eternity.

**SOPHIA.** Why?

**PHILO.** Because it is necessary for the formless to have existed before the formed. If you, O Sophia, see a wooden statue, would you not judge that the wood existed in a state lacking the form of a statue before it was shaped into one?

**SOPHIA.** Yes, certainly.

**PHILO.** And so, chaos must be found formless before the world is formed. Thus, the formation of the world shows its novelty and its being newly made; and the formless state of that from which it was made shows not novelty, but rather eternal antiquity. It follows, then, and we must grant, that just as the formed world was made newly, so we must grant that the formless chaos was never "new"; rather, it has had its being from eternity. You will therefore recognize the reason for that saying of the ancients, that nothing comes from nothing <note>original: "niente fa niente," the classical principle *ex nihilo nihil fit*.</note>; for "to make" implies a new formation, and form is relative to the formless from which it is made:

**PHILO.** In no way does he want the heavens and the stars to have substantial matter; for if they had it, they would be generable and corruptible like the lower bodies. Rather, they are only "eternal body," which acts as matter for movement, but not for generation.

...as intellectual beings, and the angels, and the pure intellects—how do they fare in this worldly corruption?

**PHILO.** If they are not composed of matter and form, and have no part in Chaos <term>Chaos: in this context, the primal "mother" or material principle of the universe.</term>, they are found separate from bodies in their own essences, contemplating the divinity. As our Albenzubron <note>Solomon ibn Gabirol (c. 1021–1058), a Jewish Neoplatonic philosopher known in the Latin world as Avicebron.</note> posits in his book *The Source of Life* <note>original: "de fonte uite"; referring to the famous philosophical work *Fons Vitae*.</note>, they too will return their portion to each of the two parents in the fifty-thousandth year. These forms are preserved most luminously within the highest Ideas <term>Ideas: the eternal, divine archetypes or patterns of all things existing in the mind of God.</term> of the divine intellect until their new return in the universal creation and generation of the universe. For at that time, Chaos, having been impregnated by the divinity, germinates material substances informed by all the Ideas. This occurs in the lower world—which is corporeal and subject to successive generation and corruption; in the celestial world—which is corporeal and moves circularly without successive generation and corruption; and in the intellectual world—consisting of incorporeal substantial matters that are immobile, ungenerated, and incorruptible. -># ON LOVE #<-

...because as I have already understood from you, the astronomers <term>astronomers: the original Italian "astrologi" referred to both astronomers and astrologers, as the study of the stars and their influence were not yet separate disciplines.</term> say that it makes one revolution in thirty-six thousand years, and some say in more than forty thousand. If the life of the world is no more than forty thousand years, it could make only a little more than one revolution in its entire lifespan, which seems strange.

**PHILO.** According to them, the entire life of the world and the rest of the universe lasts no longer than the time of a single revolution of the eighth sphere <term>eighth sphere: in the old model of the universe, this was the sphere containing the "fixed stars," which was thought to rotate very slowly over thousands of years.</term>. For although the first astronomers set it at thirty-six thousand years, and others even more ancient at less, the verification of the most recent ones—to whom we grant more faith because of their longer experience and observation—places one of its revolutions at forty thousand years. The theologians say, therefore, that the life of the world is as long as it takes the eighth sphere to make one revolution; and once that is completed, it dissolves along with everything else. The forms return to the divinity, and the matters return to Mother Chaos.

Chaos, resting for a thousand years, is impregnated once more by the divine intellect, which is filled with all its Ideas. Then, after fifty thousand years <note>This "Great Jubilee" of 50,000 years (7 cycles of 7,000 years plus a final rest) is a concept derived from Jewish Kabbalah that Leone Ebreo is blending with Greek philosophy.</note>, it returns to bring forth the heavens, the earth, and the other things of the universe. The astronomers, noting this, say that when the eighth sphere revolves once, all things return to how they were at the beginning.

*...our intellect cannot comprehend the divinity, which infinitely exceeds it in its own intellectual nature: you would not call the eye, or a mirror, a liar if it does not encompass the Sun in all its brilliance and greatness, or fire in its vastness and burning nature. Just as it is necessary for our intellect to multiply the one into three, so too must that threefold nature possess a sequence within it; otherwise, they would remain three separate natures and not one alone. Furthermore, our intellect would then be deceptive; it cannot imagine unity through multiplication unless that multiplication preserves unity through a unifying production <note>The author argues that for the mind to see God as "Three-in-One," there must be a logical flow or "production" between the parts that binds them together.</note>. This is why I told you that within the Godhead, the mind (or loving wisdom) derives eternally from the beloved beauty, and the love of both was born eternally from the beloved beauty as from a father, and from the wise lover as from a mother. I say that the lover was *produced* rather than *born*, because it did not have both parents necessary for a birth, but only a single ancestor—just as Eve our mother was produced from Adam the father <note>A reference to the Biblical account of Eve being formed from Adam's rib, signifying a derivation from a single source rather than a sexual birth.</note>, and as Chaos (the common mother of matter) <note>original: "Chaos". In this philosophical context, it refers to the primal, unformed matter of the universe.</note> was produced from the Divine Intellect, who is the universal father. But I say that Love was *born*, because it was produced by a beloved father and a loving mother—just as all men come from Adam and Eve, and the whole world from the Intellect and from mat—

*...how the world was created by God the creator, it should be clear to you that with God was the place where love was born.*

Was it in the corruptible <note>The "corruptible" world refers to the earthly realm below the moon, where all things are subject to change, decay, and death.</note>, the celestial <note>The celestial realm refers to the heavens, stars, and planets, which Renaissance thinkers believed were made of a "fifth element" and were not subject to decay.</note>, or the angelic <note>The "angelic world" refers to the realm of pure spiritual intellects, the highest level of created existence.</note>? PHI. The more clearly a question is stated, the less debatable the answer becomes. I tell you that love was first born in the angelic world, and from there it was shared with the celestial and the corruptible worlds.

SO. What reason leads you to this conclusion?

PHI. Since love proceeds—as I have told you—from beauty, then where beauty is most immense, most ancient, and co-eternal, there love must have been born first.

SO. It seems you wish to deceive me.

PHI. In what way?

SO. Because you tell me that where beauty is, there is love; yet you have already shown me that love exists where beauty is lacking <note>This refers to the Socratic idea that love is a form of "desire," and one only desires what one does not already possess.</note>.

PHI. I do not deceive you; you are the one deceiving yourself. I did not tell you that love consists *within* beauty, but that it proceeds *from* it. Love is found where the beauty that causes it is present—not that it resides *in* that beauty itself, but in the one who lacks it,

**PHI.** Therefore, in the angelic realm love is more perfect, and it had its origin there first.

Reason would therefore dictate that where the lack is greater, love should be born—that is, in the inferior world. Thus, knowledge is more closely associated with beauty than with the lack of it, and the greater it is, the less it remains

P H I. The deficiency of any perfection can exist in <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "in atto"; the state of currently being or possessing a quality.</note> alone, while the <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: "potentia"; the inherent capacity to achieve or receive a quality that is not yet present.</note> for that perfection remains; this is what is primarily called "deficiency." However, a portion of water is just as much deprived of the form of a statue in actuality as it is deprived of it in potentiality; for a statue cannot be made from water as it can from wood. That first kind of lack, which is not stripped of potentiality, is called deficiency; this other kind, which lacks both the act and the potentiality, is called absolute privation. 

And in natural things, the <term>prime matter</term> <note>The fundamental, formless "stuff" of the universe in Aristotelian philosophy, which desires to take on different forms.</note> that exists in fire or in water, even if it lacks the form and essence of air in actuality, does not lack it in potentiality; for from fire, air can be made, and likewise from water. Nonetheless, that matter lacks the form of a star, of the sun, of the moon, or anything celestial, not only in actuality but also in potentiality; for prime matter has no potentiality nor possibility for the heavens or the stars. 

This difference exists in the deficiency of beauty between the angelic world and the <term>corruttibile</term> <note>The physical world, subject to change and decay.</note> world: in the angels, their lack is a deficiency in actuality only, but they do not lack the knowledge and inclination toward it—which is like the potentiality in prime matter. And just as in prime matter the lack of the actual form gives it an inclination and desire for every form for which it has potential, so too the angelic knowledge and inclination toward the supreme beauty—which they lack—gives them ins- <note>The text continues on the next page, likely to "instills" or "inspires."</note>

### DIALOGO III.

<meta>catchword: its beauty</meta>

...without interposition <note>The text completes the thought that Moses achieved a direct union without intermediaries.</note>, that which while living could not be: for we hold that not only Moses in death was joined <term>coppulato</term> <note>original: "coppulato"; a technical term in Renaissance philosophy describing the intimate intellectual union between the human soul and the Divine.</note> immediately with the divinity, but many of the other prophets and holy fathers have also achieved this in death, even if no one other than Moses achieved it during their life.

**SOPHIA**: I have sufficiently understood the solution to the first doubt; I would like you to solve the second for me: how can it be that the angel exists in a state of potentiality through a desiring knowledge toward infinite beauty, which is impossible for it to acquire in actuality?

**PHILO**: It is impossible for the finite to become infinite, just as it is impossible for the creature to be made the creator. Regarding such an acquisition, no potentiality is found in the souls of the blessed; rather, they are in potentiality to be joined and united with the infinite beauty of God, even though they themselves are finite. In this, the knowledge they possess of His immense beauty serves them, and love and inclination direct them toward it.

**SOPHIA**: How can the infinite be known by the finite? And how can infinite beauty be imprinted upon a finite mind?

**PHILO**: This is not strange at all, because the thing known resides and is imprinted in the knower according to the mode and nature of the knower, and not according to the nature of the thing known. Observe how the entire hemisphere <note>The visible sky or horizon.</note> is seen by the eye and is imprinted within the tiniest pupil—not according to its celestial magnitude and nature, but according to the capacity of the size and power of the pupil. In this same way, infinite beauty is imprinted upon the finite angelic or blessed mind, not according to the mode of its own infinity, but according to the finite capacity of the mind that knows it. Just as the eye of the Eagle sees—and the bright and great sun is transfigured directly within it—not as the sun is in itself, but as the eye of the Eagle is capable of receiving it. There is another kind of knowledge of the immense beauty...

For he does not find it problematic that the coordinated multitude of the universe’s essences should depend immediately upon the one and most simple God; considering that everything is united like the limbs of a single individual human, and through that total unity, all its parts can depend together upon the simplest divine unity. In the divine mind, the entire universe is modeled and shaped, like the form of a crafted object in the mind of the craftsman. This form, within God, does not imply a multiplication of His essence; rather, on His part, it is one. Thus, the **Divine Ideas**, in comparison to created essences, are many; but by being in the divine mind, they are one with it.

But he says that this impression, although it is immediate in everything, is nevertheless graduated by rank according to "more" or "less." For in the first intelligence, divine beauty is impressed more worthily, spiritually, and perfectly—with a greater conformity as a likeness—than in the second; and in the second more than in the third, and so on successively until the human intellect, which is the last of the intelligences. # ON LOVE.

...down to the sphere of the Moon, and reaching **prime matter** <term>Prime Matter: In Aristotelian philosophy, this is the most basic, formless "stuff" that has the potential to become any physical thing but has no form of its own.</term>, upon which all the **Ideas** of **divine beauty** are still imprinted—just as they are in each of the **moving intelligences** <term>Moving Intelligences: Spiritual beings or angels believed to guide the rotation of the celestial spheres.</term> and the souls of the heavens, and as they are in the human **agent intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: The part of the human mind that actively processes sensory information into abstract knowledge.</term> and the wise. However, in matter, these Ideas do not appear with such clarity and brilliance; rather, they appear in a shadowy way—that is, as a physical potentiality. 

The way divine beauty is imprinted upon **prime matter** (relative to the celestial bodies) is similar to how it is imprinted upon the human **possible intellect** <term>Possible Intellect: Also called the "potential" intellect; the capacity of the human mind to receive and store knowledge, which starts as a blank slate.</term> (relative to all other actualized intellects). There is no other difference between these two types of impressions, except that in prime matter all the formal Ideas are imprinted as a *physical* potential (since matter is the lowest of all physical things), whereas in the possible intellect they are all imprinted not as a physical, but as a *spiritual*—that is, intellectual—potential. 

According to this successive graduation of the impression of divine beauty, there follows a corresponding **love** and **desire** for that beauty within the intellectual world. This occurs step by step, from the first intelligence down to the human possible intellect, which is the lowest and most humble of human intellectual powers. 

In the physical world—where love depends upon the intellectual world—this same progression occurs. It starts from the first and highest heaven and moves gradually down to **prime matter**. Just as each of the celestial spheres moves continuously in a circle without rest because of the insatiable love they have for divine beauty (seeking to participate in it and enjoy it more fully), so too does prime matter move. Driven by an insatiable desire to participate in divine beauty through the reception of forms, matter moves continuously from one form to another in a circular motion of **generation and corruption** <term>Generation and Corruption: The natural cycle of birth/creation and death/decay.</term> without ever ceasing. 

I could tell you many more particulars about each of these two opinions regarding the succession of essences and **love**...

### DIALOGUE III.

...as father, and the other as mother of **honest love**: just as Venus, through her conjunction and the power of Mars, begets excessive and libidinous human desires, so through her conjunction and marriage with **Jove** she makes him honest and virtuous.

**SOPHIA**: I understand in what way honest love is the son of Jove and Venus: tell me now why they call him a **twin**?

**FILONE**: **Plato** recounts a speech by **Pausanias** in the *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio"; Plato's famous dialogue on the nature of love</note>, saying that love is a twin because in effect there are two loves, just as there are two Venuses: for every Venus is a mother of love, and since there are two Venuses, there must also be two loves. And because the first is the **Great Venus**, celestial and divine, her son is **honest love**. Of the other, who is the inferior, libidinous Venus, the son is **base love** <note>original: "amore brutto"; literally "ugly love," referring to vulgar or purely carnal desire</note>, and therefore love is a twin—honest and base.

**SOPHIA**: Then this twin love is not solely honest, as you said.

**FILONE**: That one [the base love] is joined in the **Twin Cupids** as the son of the inferior Venus and Mars, together with the love who is the son of the Great Venus and Jove; but let us follow those who define the **Twin Love** as something other than that **Cupid**—that is, the one who is the son of Jove and the Great Venus; and this is **Honest Love**.

**SOPHIA**: How then is the honest love alone a twin?

**FILONE**: They posit this love to be a twin because, as I have said, honest love exists in both corporeal and spiritual things: in the former through the moderation of the little, and in the latter through all possible effort and growth. And whoever is honest in one is honest in the other, for, as **Aristotle** says, every wise person is good, and every good person is wise <note>A reference to the Aristotelian idea that true virtue requires both intellectual and moral excellence</note>, so that he is a twin, existing simultaneously in the corporeal and in the spiritual. Furthermore, such a name applies to both amicable love and honest love...

...other gods, after various opinions, it seemed to him <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods</note> that he should not destroy them, because if the human race were gone, there would be no one to honor the gods, nor did it seem right to leave them in their arrogance, because to tolerate it would be a disgrace to the divine ones. Around it he left some wrinkles made by the **scars** of the incision, so that man, seeing them, would remember the sin and the punishment.

**SO.** What then do you intend to signify by this opposition of words?

**PHI.** It means that Adam—that is, the first man, whom God created on the sixth day of the creation—being a human individual <term>human subject (supposto): a philosophical term referring to a distinct individual substance or person</term>, contained in himself both male and female without division. One time He calls him in the singular, "Adam," one man; the other time He calls him in the plural, "male and female He created them," to denote that while being one individual, he contained male and female together. Thus, the ancient Hebrew commentators in the Chaldean language <note>original: "lingua caldea"; referring to Aramaic, the language of the Targums and many early Jewish mystical commentaries</note> comment here, saying: Adam was created as two persons, on one side male, on the other female. And the text declares this at the end, saying that God created Adam male and female, and called their name Adam, which declared that Adam alone contained both of them, and that at first, an individual made of both was called Adam. For the female was never called Eve until she was divided from her male, Adam. So, according to the manner of the Hebrew history, it was necessary for the division to precede the sin; but the Platonic fable, although it is taken from the Hebrew one, is one with it yet of a different fashion, because it places the sin in the joined human for wanting to fight against the gods; whence, as punishment for his arrogance, he was incised and divided into two, male and female. He warns then that one must not sin, because then every "half" of man would be further divided, and each would remain only a quarter of a man. This means that if the intellectual part is not united, but rather divided by imperfect knowledge and misguided advice, it remains imperfect and weak by nature; for it is unity that makes it vigorous and perfect, while division strips it of its perfection and vigor. 

Similarly, the corporeal part is perfect when it is united in seeking what is necessary, but when it is divided by the pursuit of superfluous and insatiable things, it remains imperfect and fragile. In such a way, through this division of each of its parts, man fails to achieve not only that first intellectual union of the **Androgynous** <term>Androgynous: From the Greek *andros* (man) and *gynē* (woman); refers to the mythical four-legged, four-armed beings described by Aristophanes in Plato’s *Symposium*.</term>, but also fails to be even a "half," as is required for human life. Instead, he remains a "half of a half" <note>This refers to the idea that if a person's soul and body are both fragmented by vice, they lose the integrity required to be a complete human being.</note> by following a lewd and sinful life. 

This is what the **Platonic fable** signifies allegorically; the other details he writes about—the method of dividing, the consultation, and such—are ornaments of the story, intended to make it more beautiful and lifelike.

...of love. **PHILO**: The interpretation that we derive from this allegory regarding our objective—the birth of love—is that all human loves and desires are born from the reciprocal division of the intellect and the human body. Because the intellect, being inclined toward its body (as the male is toward the female), desires and loves the things pertaining to it; and if these are necessary and moderate, they are honorable desires and loves, characterized by their moderation and balance. But if they are superfluous, they are lustful and dishonest inclinations and sinful acts.

Furthermore, the body, by loving the intellect—as a wife loves her husband—is uplifted in desiring the perfections of the intellect. It strives through the senses, through the eyes, through the ears, and through sensation, imagination, and memory to acquire what is necessary for correct knowledge and eternal intellectual <term>habits: Here, "habits" (habiti) refers to ingrained mental dispositions or virtues that allow the mind to function at its highest level.</term>, through which the human intellect achieves its happiness. These are absolutely honorable desires and loves; and the more ardent they are, the more praiseworthy and perfect they become.

In this way, **Plato** has shown us the birth of love—specifically of all human loves. He makes the intellectual part the progenitor, acting as the father, and the corporeal part acting as the mother. The first love of man is this mutual, individual bond between the one part and the other, just like the love that exists between male and female. Following this first-born love, all other human desires and loves for all things are born from these two parents. These are categorized into three species: they are either intellectual, which are absolutely honorable (such as those of man when he was joined and whole in his first happy life in **Paradise** <note>The speaker is harmonizing Plato's myth of the original human with the biblical state of Adam in Eden before the Fall.</note>), or they are entirely physical, necessary, and moderate...

...perfection not in act, but in potential <note>This refers to the Aristotelian distinction between *potentiality* (having the capacity to become something) and *actuality* (the state of being fully realized).</note>. And thus, the intellect within a physical body <note>original: *corpo generabile*; a body capable of being born and dying</note> is a <term>potential form</term> and a <term>possible intellect</term>. Because it is an intellect, it recognizes beautiful things; but because it exists in a state of potential, it lacks the possession of those things and desires <term>actual beauty</term>. This is why it is said to be the midpoint between the beautiful and the ugly. This is because the possible intellect and material forms are the midpoint between pure matter (which is totally formless) and those separate forms and <term>angelic intelligences</term> that are "in act" and are truly beautiful.

For this reason, Diotima assigns to Love both the conditions and the workings <note>original: *machinationi*</note> of needy corporeal matter—its mortal, variable, and imperfect mother—as well as the intellectual and perfect conditions of the flowing pure intellect—its father. She portrays Love as "philosophizing" <note>original: *philosophante*; literally "acting as a lover of wisdom"</note> rather than "wise." This is because the possible intellect desires wisdom and has the potential for it, but is not "wise in act" in the same way the angelic intellect is.

Thus, in this fable, Diotima showed that the possible intellect participates in the <term>agent intellect</term> <note>The "Active Intellect" that illuminates the human mind, often associated with the divine or angelic realm in Neoplatonic thought.</note>, which exists in an angelic or divine act. She showed that its potentiality does not arise from its own intellectual nature, as some believe, but only from its companionship with needy matter, which is deprived of all "act" and is pure potential. 

She also taught that the first producer of generated love is "generated beauty," and its true parents are the knowledge of beauty (which is its father) and the lack of beauty (which is its mother). For whatever is loved and desired must first be known as beautiful, and it must be lacking—or at least be capable of being lost—so that one desires to preserve it forever. Thus, you see, Sophia, that the father of universal love in the lower world is the know- <note>The sentence continues onto the next page, likely completing the word "knowledge" (*conoscimento*).</note>

...and shows that beauty is proper to bodies; and improper, and by similitude <note>by analogy or likeness</note>, to that of the incorporeal <note>spiritual or non-physical beings</note>.

**SOPHIA:** These also possess the beauty of the circular figure, which is the most beautiful of figures, which is whole in itself and contains parts. 

**PHILO:** The circular figure is indeed beautiful in itself, but its beauty is not the proportion of the parts to one another, nor to the whole: because its parts are equal and <term>homogeneous</term> <note>original: *homogenie*; of the same kind or nature throughout</note>, in which no proportion <note>in the sense of a ratio between differing things</note> exists. Nor is the beauty of the circular figure that which makes the Sun, the Moon, and the stars beautiful; for if it were so, every <term>orbicular</term> <note>original: *orbiculare*; spherical or globe-shaped</note> body would have the beauty of the Sun. Rather, their beauty is <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *lucidita*; radiant brightness or the quality of shedding light</note>, which in itself is not a figure, nor does it have proportionate parts. 

And thus the flaming fire, and the gleaming gold, and the lucid and precious gems would not be beautiful: because all these are simple, and the parts and the whole are of one nature, without proportionate diversity. Furthermore, according to them, only the whole would be beautiful, and none of the parts would be beautiful, except in comparison to the whole. Furthermore, you will sometimes see a face be beautiful, and at another time not, even though the proportion of the parts to the whole remains exactly the same. It appears, then, that beauty is not in the proportions of the parts. And beyond that, what is more: according to them, lovely colors would not be beautiful...

And thus in the sense of hearing, a sweet voice would not be called beautiful (as it is commonly called); and if they insist that the beauty of music is the <term>concordance of parts</term> <note>the harmonious arrangement of different musical notes or voices</note>, what then shall **intellectual beauty** be? So, if you consider it well, you will find that although beauty is found in proportionate and concordant things, beauty is something *beyond* their proportion; wherefore it is found not only in proportionate composites, but even more so in simple things.

**SOPHIA:** Therefore, could disproportionate things be beautiful?

**PHILO:** Not at all; for disproportionate things are defective and evil, and no evil thing is beautiful. But nevertheless, proportion is not beauty itself. This is because those things that are neither proportionate nor disproportionate—because they are not <term>composites</term> <note>objects made of multiple parts or elements</note>—are found to be most beautiful. Furthermore, among proportionate and concordant things, there are some that are not beautiful, because not every beautiful and good thing is proportionate. 

Moreover, in evil things, one still finds proportion and concordance. It is a saying among merchants that the greedy man and the swindler "accord" quickly; and fear accompanies cruelty, and prodigality accompanies robbery. Therefore, not every beautiful thing is proportionate, nor is every proportionate thing beautiful, as these people have thought.

**SOPHIA:** What then is the beauty of corporeal things, which makes well-proportioned figures and bodies beautiful, if beauty is not proportion?

**PHILO:** Know that **matter**, the foundation of all <term>inferior bodies</term> <note>original: *corpi inferiori*; in the Renaissance worldview, these are the physical objects of the Earthly realm, subject to decay, as opposed to the "superior" heavenly bodies</note>, is in itself deformed, and the mother of all deformity in them; but

<meta>catchword: but</meta>

<summary>Philo argues that beauty is a spiritual quality existing beyond physical proportions, pointing out that even evil things can be "proportioned" and that the highest beauty exists in simple, divine forms without parts.</summary>

...ears bring it to them? PHI. You will see the answer to this, along with the solution to your doubt, if you will let me speak. You know that physical beauties are degrees of form; and I have already told you that all abstract forms <note>In this context, "forms" refers to the ideal or spiritual blueprints of things, a core concept in Platonic philosophy.</note> exist spiritually in a unified order within the **Soul of the World**, of which our rational soul is an image. This is because the soul's essence is a latent configuration of all those spiritual forms, imprinted upon it by the Soul of the World, which is its exemplary origin. 

This latent configuration is what Aristotle calls *potentiality* <term>potentiality: the capacity for something to become manifest or "actual," like a seed's potential to become a tree</term>, a universal preparation within the intellect that makes it possible to receive and understand all forms and essences. For if all these forms were not already within the soul in a potential or latent way, the soul would not be able to receive them or understand each one of them in actuality and through pre-existence. 

Plato says that our reasoning and understanding is a reminiscence <note>The theory of anamnesis: the idea that the soul "remembers" truths it knew before it was joined with a physical body.</note> of things pre-existing in the soul, hidden by a kind of oblivion. This "oblivion" is the same thing as Aristotle’s *potentiality* and the latent state I am describing to you. 

Thus, you will realize that forms and species <note>original: "specie" — here meaning the mental images or essences of things.</note> do not simply jump from physical bodies into our soul, because it is impossible for something to migrate from one subject to another. However, when these forms are presented to us through the senses, they cause those same forms and essences—which were already shining within our soul—to shine forth once more. This "shining forth" is what Aristotle calls the "act of understanding" and Plato calls "memory"; though their words differ, their meaning is one and the same. 

Our soul, then, is full of formal beauties; indeed, these beauties are its very essence. If they are hidden within it, this latency does not come from the intellect itself (which makes these beauties essential), but from the soul’s binding and union with the human body and matter. The first face, directed toward the intellect, is the intellectual faculty. Through this, the soul discourses with universal and spiritual knowledge, extracting intellectual forms and essences from particular and sensible bodies, thereby always transforming the corporeal world into the intellectual. The second face, directed toward the body, is the sense. This is a particular knowledge of corporeal things, joined with and mingled with the materiality of the physical things being known. 

These two faces have contrary or opposite motions. Just as our soul, with its first face—that is, **rational knowledge**—makes the corporeal into the incorporeal, so too with the second face—or **sensible knowledge**—by drawing near to physical bodies and mixing with them, it draws the incorporeal down to the corporeal. 

Corporeal beauties are known by our soul through these two modes of knowledge, using both faces: that is, sensually and bodily, or rationally and intellectually. Depending on which of these two knowledges of corporeal beauty is used, a corresponding love is awakened in the soul: through sensible knowledge comes **sensual love**, and through rational knowledge comes **spiritual love**. Aristotle wants to be more moderate in this matter, because it seems to him that the supreme perfection of the **Artificer** <note>God, viewed as the supreme craftsman.</note> must produce works that are perfect in themselves. Therefore, he holds that the **primary substances** <term>Primary substances: In Aristotelian logic, these are individual, concrete things (like a specific person or a specific tree) rather than abstract categories.</term> are the individuals, and that in each of them the essence of the **species** <note>The general category or "kind" of thing.</note> is preserved. Regarding these species, he does not believe they are the "Ideas" (which are the causes of realities), but rather only **intellectual concepts** of our rational soul, taken from the substance and essence that is found in each of the real individuals. Because of this, he calls those universal concepts **secondary substances** <term>Secondary substances: The species or genera to which individual things belong (e.g., "Humanity" or "Animal").</term>, because they are abstracted by our intellect from the primary individuals.

He does not want the Ideas to be primary substances, as Plato says, nor even secondary ones, but rather the **primary causes** of all corporeal substances and of all their essences composed of matter and form. They believed that all beauty, essence, and substance resided in the **Ideas** <term>Ideas: In this philosophical tradition, these are the perfect, eternal forms or blueprints of all things that exist in the Divine Mind.</term> and nothing existed in the corporeal world. Seeing that for this reason they were becoming negligent in the knowledge of corporeal things—and in their acts, motions, and natural alterations, as well as the causes of their generation and decay—he realized that such negligence would result in a defect and lack of knowledge even of the abstract spiritual principles. This is because a deep knowledge of effects ultimately leads to a perfect knowledge of their causes. Therefore, it seemed to him time to temper the extreme in this matter, which perhaps in its progress might have exceeded the Platonic goal. He demonstrated, as I have told you, that there are properly in the corporeal world essences and substances produced and caused by the Ideas, and that there are in it also true beauties, although they are dependent upon the purest and most perfect Ideal ones. Thus, Plato was a doctor who cured a sickness of excess, and Aristotle was a doctor who preserved the health already introduced by Plato's work through the use of temperament.

### DIALOGUE III ###

...not in their perfect causes, but are inherent in the effects precisely because they are effects; and through their nature as effects, they are far distant from the perfection of the cause. Therefore, defects arise in them that do not pre-exist in, nor originate from, their causes. 

SOPHIA: On the contrary, it seems that good causes produce good effects, and that effects ought to be so similar to their causes that the causes can be known through them. 

PHILO: Although a good effect comes from a good cause, the goodness and perfection of the effect do not for that reason match those of the cause; and though the effect resembles its cause, it does not equal it in its perfecting qualities. It is certainly true that the perfection of the cause induces a perfection in the effect that is proportionate to that effect, but not equal to the perfection of the cause itself; for if it were, the effect would be the cause and not the effect, or the cause would be the effect and not the cause. It is true that an effect is as good and perfect *as an effect* as the cause is *as a cause*; however, they are not simply equal in perfection. Rather, the effect falls far short of the perfection of its cause, and for this reason, defects are found in it that are not found in the cause. 

SOPHIA: I understand the reasoning, but I would like an example. 

PHILO: You know that the corporeal world <note>The "corporeal world" refers to the entire physical, material universe.</note> proceeds from the incorporeal as a proper effect from its cause and <term>artisan: the "sommo opifice" or divine architect/craftsman</term>; nevertheless, the corporeal does not contain the perfection of the incorporeal, and you see how far the body falls short of the intellect. If you find many defects in the body, such as <term>dimension: the physical property of taking up space and having size</term>, <term>division: the capacity to be broken into parts, unlike the indivisible soul</term>, and in some things <term>alteration: the process of change or shifting states</term> and <term>corruption: the natural decay or dissolution of physical matter</term> <note>These four properties—dimension, division, alteration, and corruption—were considered "defects" by Neoplatonists because they imply a lack of the eternal, unchanging stability found in the Divine.</note>, you must not judge that these things pre-exist in their intellectual causes in a defective way. Rather, you should judge that these exist in the effect only because of the lack...

### DIALOGUE III.

<note>Sophia continues:</note> if it is necessary to understand it, I pray that you communicate it to me; even though I may not deserve it through my own acquisition.

**PHILO.** There is another way to answer your doubt, by granting you that the **divine wisdom** and **intellect**—the **Idea** <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" is the eternal, perfect archetype or blueprint of a thing that exists in the divine mind.</note> of the universe—is in some way distinct and different from the **highest God**; for **Plato** seems to affirm this. For he holds that the **divine intellect** and **wisdom** (which is the **Ideal Word** <note>original: "uerbo Ideale"; likely a reference to the *Logos*, the mediating principle between God and the created world.</note>) is not properly the **highest God**, nor is it entirely something else or distinct from Him. Rather, it is something of His, depending on and emanating from Him, yet not separated or really distinct from Him, just as the light is to the Sun. 

And this intellect of His, or wisdom, he calls the **Maker of the world** <note>original: "opifice del mondo"; the Demiurge or craftsman who shapes the universe according to the divine plan.</note>: the **Idea** of it, containing within its simplicity and unity all the essences and forms of the universe. These he calls **Ideas**; meaning that within the highest wisdom are contained all the notions of the universe and all its parts, from which notions all things are jointly produced and known. 

The **highest God** (whom he sometimes calls the **highest good**) he says is above the first intellect—that is, the origin from which the first intellect emanates. And he says that He is not **Being**, but **above Being** <note>original: "non è Ente, ma sopra Ente"; this reflects Neoplatonic thought where the ultimate Source (The One) is so transcendent that it precedes the very category of existence or being.</note>; for the first essence is the first Being, and the first intellect is the first Idea. And he finds Him so hidden from the pure, abstract human mind that he can hardly find a name to impose upon Him; therefore, most of the time, he names Him ***He Himself*** <note>original: "Ipse"; Latin for "Himself." This signifies God as pure subjectivity without external attributes.</note>, without any other property of a name, fearing that no name the human mind could produce, or the material tongue could utter, would be capable of any property of the highest God. 

And indeed, some **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> wished to follow this path (though imperfectly), such as **Avicenna** <note>The Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note>, and **Algazali** <note>The Persian philosopher and theologian Al-Ghazali (c. 1058–1111).</note>, and our **Rabbi Moses** <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the influential Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note>, and their followers, who say...

PHI. Since I am a follower of the Mosaic law <note>original: "mosaico," referring to the laws and traditions of Moses/Judaism</note>, in theological wisdom I embrace this second path, for it is truly Mosaic theology; and Plato, as one who had greater knowledge of this ancient wisdom than Aristotle, followed it. He reached as far as the highest wisdom and the first beauty; and his intellect, being satisfied with that and without seeing any further, he affirmed that this was the first <term>incorporeal principle</term> <note>a beginning or source that has no physical body</note> of all things.

Instead, he made that beauty the second principle of the universe, dependent on the Supreme God, the principle of all things. And although Plato was Aristotle’s teacher for many years, in those divine matters Plato himself, being a disciple of our elders, learned from better teachers—and learned more than Aristotle learned from him; for the disciple of a disciple cannot reach the level of the disciple of the master. 

Even though Aristotle was extremely subtle, I believe that in abstraction his intellect could not elevate itself as much as Plato’s. Furthermore, he did not wish, as others did, to believe his master regarding what the natural powers of his own intellect could not demonstrate to him.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue where Philo (PHI) is explaining to Sophia (SO) that Plato’s philosophical views on Beauty and Creation are actually rooted in the much older Mosaic (Jewish) tradition. He is specifically comparing how Moses, Plato, and Aristotle view the relationship between God and His Wisdom.</meta>

->OF LOVE.<-

...not [learn more than Plato]; and he sees further than I do. But I would like you to show me where Moses and the other holy prophets signified this Platonic truth.

PHI. The first words that Moses wrote were: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.* And the ancient Chaldean interpretation <note>original: "interpretatione Caldea"; this refers to the *Targum*, ancient Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible used to clarify the text's meaning</note> says that where we say "in the beginning," it should be: *with wisdom God created the heaven and the earth.* And because Wisdom is called "Beginning" in Hebrew—as Solomon said, "The beginning is wisdom" <note>A reference to Proverbs 4:7</note>—and the word "in" can also mean "with" <note>In Hebrew, the prefix *Be-* in *Bereshit* can be translated as either "In" or "By means of/With"</note>. So, the first words of the wise Moses denoted the three levels of Beauty: God, Wisdom, and the World. common. This formal part is their appropriate moderation <note>original: "temperamento" — the balanced mixture or moderation of qualities.</note> toward the necessary and excellent ends for which they are directed: the sustenance of the individual and the preservation of the species. 

And so it happens in the category of the **love of the useful** <note>original: "utile" — love based on utility or benefit.</note>: that which is purely useful and stripped of the honest—meaning immoderate and disproportionate to the needs of life and virtuous works—is only good and beautiful in appearance; in reality, it is bad and harmful, such as **greed** <note>original: "cupidità"</note> and **avarice**. But when it is tempered and appropriate to these two ends <note>the preservation of the individual and the species</note>, it is truly good and beautiful; it then enters into both categories of love: the useful and the honest. This is because its matter belongs to the useful, while the form of its moderation belongs to the honest.

**SO.** Therefore, the love of the honest is sometimes materially composed of the pleasurable, and sometimes of the useful. Now, would there perhaps be any love that is both materially and formally honest, without taking anything from either of the other two categories?

**PHI.** The love of the honest is to love the moral and intellectual virtues. Because moral virtues concern human actions, their matter must follow the nature of those operations in which the virtue exists. Thus, the virtue of conti= <note>The text breaks here; the catchword indicates the word is "continenza" or continence/self-control.</note>

In this, the noble lover tastes the very possession of the useful as a delight. 

And thus all the other **moral virtues** <note>The virtues concerning human behavior and emotions, such as courage or justice, as opposed to intellectual pursuits.</note> that concern human actions—such as **fortitude**, **justice**, **prudence**, and others—have the matter of an active nature, and their form is the noble habit of its moderation. 

But the **intellectual virtues** are all noble by nature, and they have no material element; for they do not revolve around bodily acts or delights from which they might take any matter, but around eternal things, separated from bodies and understood by the intellect. Therefore, they are all intellectual forms without the company of matter; they are pure and truly noble in themselves, and not by participation like the others. Because of this, **Plato** calls the love of these things **divine**.

<margin>PHI.</margin> He divides the genres of love into three, like Aristotle, but in a different way: these are **bestial love**, **human love**, and **divine love**. -># ON LOVE.<-

...how was love born in the universe? For in that case, it does not seem as easy to me to establish delight as the goal, as it is in the specific loves of men and other animals. PHI. It is high time I told you. You know that once, the world was produced by the supreme Creator through love; for when the supreme Good <note>original: "sommo buono" — referring to God as the Platonic Form of the Good.</note> beheld His own immense beauty and loved it, and that beauty loved Him, as the supreme Beautiful, He produced or generated—in the likeness of His own beauty—the beautiful universe. For the goal of love is (as Plato says) **birth in beauty** <note>original: "parto in bello," a reference to Plato’s *Symposium*, where love is described as "procreation in beauty" (*tokos en kalō*).</note>. Therefore, the universe having been produced by its supreme Creator in the likeness or image of His immense wisdom, there was born the love of the Creator toward this universe—not as a love from the imperfect toward the perfect, but as a love from the most perfect superior toward the less perfect inferior, and as from a father to a son, or from a cause to its unique effect. 

Hence, the goal of this love is not to acquire beauty that the lover lacks, nor to find delight in union with the beloved; rather, it exists to make the beloved acquire a greater perfection, which it would lack if it did not receive it through the love of the lover. The divine Lover thus delights in the greater beauty that the beloved universe attains through His divine love. This is what happens in all loves of causes for their effects, from superiors to inferiors: from fathers to sons, from the teacher to the disciple, and from all benefactors to those they benefit. Their love is a desire for their inferior to reach the highest degree of perfection and beauty; the lover then delights in the union of that beauty with the beloved. And this delight of the lover in the perfection and beauty of the beloved is the goal of that lover's love. SO.

<summary>Philo explains that universal love originates from the Creator, who produced the world "in beauty." Unlike human love, which seeks to acquire what it lacks, divine or paternal love seeks to bestow perfection upon the beloved and delights in the beloved's resulting excellence.</summary>

This circle has two halves <note>original: "mezi"; literally "middles" or "halves" in the context of a geometric arc.</note>. **SOPHIA**: In a geometric circle <note>original: "circulo figurale"</note> it is so. But tell me, how is this found in the circle of all things? 

**PHILO**: Since the beginning and the end of the circle is the Supreme Producer, its midpoint is found by descending from Him to the lowest point most distant from His supreme perfection. For from Him first follows the angelic nature through its ordered degrees from greater to lesser; and then the celestial nature with its successive degrees from the empyrean heaven <note>The highest, most spiritual part of the physical universe in medieval cosmology.</note>, which is the greatest, down to the least, which is that of the Moon. ...who loves you. Look how he begins to speak in the singular, saying *draw me*, and immediately speaks in the plural, saying *we will run after you*; then he returns to the singular: *if the King should lead me into his chambers*; and returns to the plural to say, *we will delight and rejoice in you; we will remember your loves more than wine*. He does this to show that through the union of the **intellectual part** of man—or of the created universe—God brings happiness and delight not only to that part, but to all the parts of the universe along with it. It is for these parts that he says in the plural, *the righteous love you* <note>original: "le rettitudini t'amano"; a reference to the "upright" (recti) in Song of Songs 1:4.</note>, because they all tend toward <term>divine love</term> <note>The ultimate goal of all creation in Neoplatonic thought is to return to its source through love.</note> by means of the intellectual part. 

Thus, the work and the shining of divine love within us is what first guides us into our happy delight; and following that comes the most ardent work of our own love within us, which leads us to unite and find bliss with His supreme beauty. So that you may understand this better, consider its likeness in the relationship between two perfect lovers, a man and a woman. Even if the male lover has an ardent love for the beloved woman, he never has the boldness or the possibility of enjoying that delightful union—which is the end and goal of his love—unless she, with the rays of her loving eyes, with sweet words, with gentle bearing, with pleasing signs and affectionate gestures, shows him such a pleasure of **amorous correspondence** <note>The "correspondence" (correspondentia) is the mutual recognition and return of love between the lover and the beloved.</note> that it uplifts and enlivens his love. This makes him capable and bold enough to lead himself into that delightful union with the beloved, which is the <term>perfecting end</term> <note>The final state where the lover's potential is fully realized or "perfected" through union.</note> of his most ardent love.

**SOPHIA.** I am entirely satisfied regarding these doubts of mine. As for the obligation you had to tell me of the **birth of love**, you are now released from it with a payment no less great than the one you made me earlier concerning the **essence of love**. ### DIALOGUE III.

...desire, and then of the community of love; and in this third [dialogue] I recognize how love truly was born. I see how the love that God has for the universe, and the universe for God, were born when the universe was born, along with the reciprocal love of its parts for one another. I recognize that the principle of its birth in the produced universe is in the **angelic world** <note>In Neoplatonic cosmology, the "angelic world" or *Mundus Intelligibilis* is the first level of creation, sitting between God and the physical world.</note>, and thus I know its most noble genealogy: its parents are **knowledge** and **beauty**, and **Lucina** <note>original: "lucina"; the Roman goddess of childbirth, used here metaphorically to mean the "midwife" or the condition that brings the birth about.</note> at its birth is **lack** <note>original: "mancamento"; this refers to the Platonic idea that love is born from "Poverty" (Penia) and "Plenty" (Poros), as love always seeks what it does not have.</note>. Finally, I know that its end is the delight of the lover in the unitive enjoyment of the beloved beauty, and that of the universe in the **supreme beauty**, which is the ultimate, blissful end of all things—which may the Most High God deign to grant us. Although I believed, O Philo, that the purpose for which love was born might sometimes be to afflict and torture lovers who affectionately love their beloveds.

PHI. Although love brings with it affliction and torment, anxiety, and distress, and many other pains which it would be long to recount, these are not its proper end; rather, it is that **sweet delight** which is the opposite of these. Nonetheless, you have spoken the truth—not of every love, but only of mine toward you, for its end has never been pleasure nor delight; instead, I see that its beginning, middle, and end are nothing but sorrows, anguishes, and passions.

SO. How then does the rule fail in you? And why is yours deprived of that which every other love ought to achieve?

PHI. You may ask this of yourself, and not of me. It is my part to love you as much as my soul can contain; if you make this love sterile and deprived of its due end, do you wish for me to seek your excuse?

...who looks for yours: for since your love is stripped of the **proper end** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "end" (*telos*) is the ultimate purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> that you have assigned to love, it must be that yours is not true love, or that this is not its true end.

**PHI.** The end of every love is **delight**, and mine is a most true love, and its end is to enjoy you with **unitive delight** <note>original: "unitiua dilettatione"; a Neoplatonic concept where the goal of love is the spiritual and physical "becoming one" of the lover and the beloved.</note>: toward which end the lover and the love are intent. Nevertheless, not everyone who strives for an end acquires it—all the more so when the achievement of that end must come from the hand of another. Such is the delight of the lover: it is the end toward which his love tends, but it will never be reached unless the **reciprocal love** of his beloved leads him into it. So, that which causes my love for you to fail its end is that your reciprocal love fails in its duty; for if love was born in the whole universe and in every one of its parts, it seems to me that in you alone it was never born.

**SO.** Perhaps it was not born because it was not well sown.

**PHI.** It was not well sown because the terrain did not wish to receive the **perfect seed**.

**SO.** Then it is defective.

**PHI.** In this, yes, truly.

**SO.** Everything defective is **deformed**; how then do you love the deformed? If it is because your love seems beautiful to you, then it is not right, nor true, as you say.

**PHI.** There is nothing so beautiful that it has no defect, except for the **Supreme Beauty** <note>original: "sommo bello"; referring to God, who in this philosophical system is the only entity of pure perfection without lack.</note>: and in you there is such beauty that even if this defect—which makes me unhappy—accompanies it, your great beauty can move me to love you much more than this small defect (though quite harmful to me) can move me to hate you.

**SO.** I do not know what beauty of mine this could be, which moves you so much to love me: you have shown me that true beauty is **wisdom** <note>original: "sapientia"</note>; in me there is no other part of this than that which you offer me: in you...

And of this you cannot doubt, considering my diligence in contemplating the concepts of your mind and in enjoying your wisdom, in which I receive the greatest delight. 

Of the other, corporeal union <note>This refers to physical or sexual intimacy, which Sophia contrasts with the "purity" of intellectual or spiritual connection.</note> that lovers are accustomed to desire, I do not believe, nor would I wish, that any such desire be found in you or in me; for just as spiritual love is entirely full of good and beauty, and all its effects are fitting and salvific, so I believe that corporeal love is rather base and deformed, and its effects for the most part are troublesome and harmful. And so that I may better respond to you regarding this, tell me, I pray (as you have already promised me), about the effects of human love: which are good and laudable, and which are pernicious and blameworthy, and which of these are greater in number? <meta>This page follows the conclusion of Dialogue III and serves as the colophon—the final identifying statement of the publication. It includes the signature register, which acted as a guide for the bookbinder to ensure all printed sheets were present and in the correct order, followed by the printer's mark and publication details.</meta>

<image-desc>The printer's mark of the Aldine Press: a central anchor with a dolphin entwined around the shank. The dolphin's tail is at the top right, and its head is near the bottom left of the anchor's cross. This famous symbol represents the motto "Festina Lente" (Hasten Slowly), signifying the balance of speed and precision in the printer's craft.</image-desc>

<summary>This page concludes the volume with a printer’s register and colophon, identifying the book as a 1541 edition from the renowned Venetian press established by Aldus Manutius and continued by his sons.</summary>
